front: Why do ideal gases have no potential energy?
back: Ideal gases have no potential energy because there are no intermolecular forces in an ideal gas.

front: What is the relationship between kinetic energy and internal energy for an ideal gas?
back: For an ideal gas, internal energy is the total kinetic energy of all the particles.

front:
True or False?
As the internal energy of an ideal gas increases, the average speed of the particles increases.
back:
True.
Internal energy is directly proportional to temperature, which is directly proportional to kinetic energy. As kinetic energy increases, so does the average speed of particles.

front: State the equation for the first law of thermodynamics.
back:

Where:
• Q = energy supplied to the system by heating, measured in joules (J)
• ΔU = change in internal energy, measured in joules (J)
• W = work done on/by the system, measured in joules (J)

front: What is the sign of W when work is done on a gas?
back: When work is done on a gas, W is negative.

front: What is the sign of W when work is done by a gas?
back: When work is done by a gas, W is positive.

front: What is the sign of ΔU when a gas is heated and work is done on a gas?
back: When a gas is heated and work is done to it, its internal energy increases so ΔU is positive.

front: What is the sign of ΔU when a gas transfers heat to its surroundings and expands?
back: When a gas transfers heat away, Q is negative and when it expands it does work so Wis negative. This means its internal energy decreases so ΔU is negative.

back: Using the first law of thermodynamics:

front:
True or False?
If a gas is heated, it must expand.
back:
False.
From the first law of thermodynamics,

If a gas is heated, Q is positive, but the energy may increase the system's internal energy instead of causing expansion.
So W can be zero while the first law is still obeyed.

front: Define the entropy of a system.
back: The entropy of a system is a measure of the number of possible arrangements of the particles and their energies, i.e. it is a measure of the disorder of the system.

front: Put the three main states of matter in order from highest to lowest entropy.
back:
The three main states of matter, in order from highest to lowest entropy, are:
• Gas (highest entropy)
• Liquid
• Solid (lowest entropy)

front:
True or False?
Entropy and temperature remain constant during a change of state.
back:
False.
Temperature remains constant during a change of state, but entropy changes.

front: Does entropy increase or decrease during sublimation?
back: In sublimation, a solid becomes a gas so entropy increases.

front: Does entropy increase or decrease during freezing?
back: In freezing, a liquid becomes a solid so entropy decreases.

front: Other than changing state of matter, what are two situations in which entropy can increase?
back:
Entropy can also increase when
• A solid dissolves in a solvent
• A gas diffuses in a container

front: Define a reversible process.
back: A reversible process is one where there is no overall change in entropy as the system and its surroundings are returned to their original states.

front: Define an irreversible process.
back: An irreversible process is one that results in an increase in entropy as the system and its surroundings cannot return to their original states.

front:
True or False?
Processes occurring in real isolated systems are almost always irreversible.
back:
True.
Processes occurring in real isolated systems are almost always irreversible. The entropy of a real isolated system always increases.

front: Define an isolated system.
back: An isolated system is one in which neither matter nor energy can be transferred in or out.

front: State the equation for change in macroscopic entropy.
back:
Change in macroscopic entropy is
Where:
• ΔS = change in entropy, measured in joules per kelvin (J K⁻¹)
• ΔQ = heat given to or removed from the system, measured in joules (J)
• T = temperature of the system, measured in kelvin (K)

front: How does entropy change when heat is removed from a non-isolated system?
back: When heat is removed from a non-isolated system, its entropy can decrease locally.

front: Why can the entropy of a non-isolated system decrease?
back: The entropy of a non-isolated system can decrease because this is compensated for by an equal, or greater increase in the entropy of the surroundings.

front: What is the net change in thermal energy transferred for a reversible process?
back: For a reversible process,  therefore change in heat transferred .

front: State the equation for a system's microscopic entropy.
back:
A system's microscopic entropy is
Where:
• S = entropy, measured in joules per kelvin (J K⁻¹)
• kB = Boltzmann constant, measured in joules per kelvin (J K⁻¹)
• Ω = the number of possible microstates of the system

front: State the equation for the change in a system's microscopic entropy.
back:
A system's microscopic entropy is
Where:
• ΔS = change in entropy, measured in joules per kelvin (J K⁻¹)
• kB = Boltzmann constant, measured in joules per kelvin (J K⁻¹)
• Ω₁ = the initial number of possible microstates of the system
• Ω₂ = the final number of possible microstates of the system

front: Define the term microstate.
back: A microstate is one possible arrangement of the particles in the system.

front: State the second law of thermodynamics.
back: The second law of thermodynamics states that in every process, the total entropy of an isolated system always increases.

front: State the second law of thermodynamics in the Kelvin form.
back: The Kelvin form of the second law of thermodynamics states that when extracting energy from a heat reservoir, it is impossible to convert it all into work.

front: State the second law of thermodynamics in the Clausius form.
back: The Clausius form of the second law of thermodynamics states that thermal energy cannot spontaneously transfer from a region of lower temperature to a region of higher temperature.

front:
True or False?
Heat can be converted completely into work without flowing into a cold reservoir.
back:
False.
Heat cannot be completely converted to work, this violates the Kelvin form of the second law.

front:
True or False?
Heat cannot spontaneously flow from a cold region to a warmer region.
back:
True.
Heat cannot spontaneously flow from a cold region to a warmer region.

front: Under what condition can heat flow from a cold region to a hot region?
back: Heat can flow from a cold region to a hot region when work is done on the system.

front: State the condition for a process to be isovolumetric.
back: The condition for an isovolumetric process is  i.e. the volume remains constant.

front: State the condition for a process to be isobaric.
back: The condition for an isobaric process is  i.e. the pressure remains constant.

front: State the condition for a process to be isothermal.
back: The condition for an isothermal process is , i.e. the temperature remains constant.

front: State the condition for a process to be adiabatic.
back: The condition for an adiabatic process is , i.e. no heat is transferred into or out of the system.

front: State the equation for work done under constant pressure.
back:
The equation for work done under constant pressure is
Where:
• W is work done, measured in joules (J)
• P is pressure, measured in pascals (Pa)
• ΔV is change in volume, measured in metres-cubed (m³)

front: What region of a pressure-volume graph represents work done during a process?
back: On a pressure-volume graph, the area under a line represents the work done during that process.

front: What are two thermodynamic processes in which entropy does not change?
back:
Two thermodynamic processes in which entropy does not change are:
• Adiabatic expansion
• Adiabatic compression

front: What are three thermodynamic processes in which entropy increases?
back:
Three thermodynamic processes in which entropy increases are:
• Isobaric expansion
• Isothermal expansion
• Isovolumetric heating

front: What are three thermodynamic processes in which entropy decreases?
back:
Three thermodynamic processes in which entropy decreases are:
• Isobaric compression
• Isothermal compression
• Isovolumetric cooling

False.
On a pressure-volume graph, an isobaric process is represented with a straight horizontal line, while an adiabatic process is represented with a curve steeper than an isotherm.

front: What are the four steps of a simple heat engine?
back:
The four steps of a simple heat engine are:
• Extract heat from a hot reservoir
•  Use some of the extracted heat to perform work
• Release excess heat into a cold reservoir
• Return to initial state and repeat

front: What is the most efficient engine cycle theoretically possible?
back: The Carnot cycle is the most efficient engine cycle theoretically possible.

front: Name the thermodynamic process in the first stage of the Carnot cycle.
back: The thermodynamic process in the first stage of the Carnot cycle is isothermal expansion.

front: Name the thermodynamic process in the second stage of the Carnot cycle.
back: The thermodynamic process in the second stage of the Carnot cycle is adiabatic expansion.

front: Name the thermodynamic process in the third stage of the Carnot cycle.
back: The thermodynamic process in the third stage of the Carnot cycle is isothermal compression.

front: Name the thermodynamic process in the fourth stage of the Carnot cycle.
back: The thermodynamic process in the fourth stage of the Carnot cycle is adiabatic compression.

front: Define electric current.
back: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge carriers.

front: What are the charged particles that flow in electrical circuits?
back: The charged particles that flow in electrical circuits are electrons.

front: Define conventional current.
back: Conventional current is the flow of positive charge from the positive terminal of a cell to the negative terminal.

front: Define direct current.
back: Direct current (d.c.) flows around a circuit in one direction.

front:
True or False?
Electrons flow around a circuit towards the positive terminal, but conventional current flows around a circuit towards the negative terminal.
back:
True.
Electrons do flow around a circuit towards the positive terminal, while conventional current flows towards the negative terminal. It is electrons that actually form the current, but the idea of conventional current was in use before the electron was discovered.

front:

What is the current in the circuit?

front: Define electric potential difference.
back: Electric potential difference is the work done per unit charge on moving a positive charge between two points along the path of the current.

front:
True or False?
One volt is equal to one joule per coulomb.
back:
True.
One volt is equal to one joule per coulomb, 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.

front:
True or False?
A cell or battery provides the source of potential difference in an a.c. circuit.
back:
False.
A cell or battery provides the source of potential difference in a d.c. circuit.

front:
True or False?
Electrons are stored in the cell and flow through the wires when the circuit is closed.
back:
False.
The electrons in the circuit are the delocalised electrons in the metal of the wires and components. They flow around the closed circuit when a potential difference is applied.

front: Define the electronvolt.
back: The electronvolt is the amount of energy needed to move an electron through a potential difference of one volt.

front: What is an electrical conductor?
back: An electrical conductor is a material that allows charge (usually electrons) to flow through it easily.

front: Give one example of an electrical conductor.
back: Examples of electrical conductors are: copper; silver; aluminium; steel; gold

front: Why are metals good electrical conductors?
back: Metals are good electrical conductors because metals have delocalised electrons that flow when a potential difference is applied.

front: What is an electrical insulator?
back: An electrical insulator is a material that has no delocalised electrons, so it does not allow charge to flow easily.

front: Give one example of an electrical insulator.
back: Examples of electrical insulators are: rubber; plastic; glass; wood

front: What is static electricity?
back: Static electricity occurs when charge builds up on the surface of an insulator and is discharged when brought into contact with a conductor.

front: Define an ideal ammeter.
back: An ideal ammeter has zero resistance, such that all the current passes through it.

front: Define an ideal voltmeter.
back: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance, such that no current passes through it.

front: Define the resistance of a component.
back: The resistance of a component is the ratio of the potential difference across the component to the current flowing through it.

front: State the equation for resistance known as Ohm's law.
back:

front:
True or False?
The greater the resistance of a component, the higher the current flowing through it.
back:
False.
The greater the resistance of a component, the lower the current flowing through it.

front: State the SI base units for 1 Ω.
back: The SI base units for 1 Ω are kg m⁻² s⁻³ A⁻².

front:
True or False?
For resistance calculations, mA and kV must be converted into A and V.
back:
True.
For resistance calculations, mA and kV must be converted into A and V.

front:
True or False?
Resistance is caused by collisions between flowing electrons and the metal ions in the conductor.
back:
True.
Resistance is caused by collisions between flowing electrons and the metal ions in the conductor.

front: State the factors affecting resistance.
back: The factors affecting resistance are: material; length; cross-sectional area; temperature

front:
True or False?
The resistance of a wire is directly proportional to its length.
back:
True.
The resistance of a wire is directly proportional to its length.

front:
True or False?
The resistance of a wire is directly proportional to its cross-sectional area.
back:
False.
The resistance of a wire is inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area.

front: Define resistivity.
back: Resistivity is the electrical resistance of a conductor of unit cross-sectional area and unit length.

front: Do metals have high or low values of resistivity?
back: Metals have low values of resistivity, and insulators have high values.

front: What does the gradient of an I-V graph represent?
back: The gradient of an I-V graph represents the resistance of a component.

front: What does a linear I-V graph show?
back:
A linear I-V (current-voltage) graph shows
• the relationship between current and potential difference is directly proportional
• the resistance of the component is constant

front:
True or False?
As the current through a filament lamp increases, the resistance decreases.
back:
False.
As the current through a filament lamp increases, the resistance increases.

front: Why does the resistance of a filament lamp change when the voltage is changed?
back: The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the voltage is increased because as the voltage increases, current increases, and the lamp heats up; as the temperature increases, metal ions in the filament wire vibrate more; the number of collisions between the ions and free electrons increases

front: What are the main features of an I-V graph for a diode?
back:
The I-V graph for a diode shows they have
• a high resistance when the current flows in one direction
• a low resistance when the current flows in the opposite direction

front:
True or False?
Current is different at different points in a series circuit.
back:
False.
Current is the same everywhere in a series circuit.

front:
True or False?
In a parallel circuit, the current from the power source is larger than the current in each branch.
back:
True.
In a parallel circuit, the current from the power source is larger than the current in each branch.

front:
True or False?
The amount of current flowing in a series circuit depends on the potential difference and resistance in the circuit.
back:
True.
The amount of current flowing in any circuit depends on the potential difference and resistance in the circuit.

front:
True or False?
Current is conserved at a junction in a parallel circuit.
back:
True.
Current is conserved at a junction in a parallel circuit because charge is always conserved.

front:
True or False?
Current always splits equally at a junction in a parallel circuit.
back:
False.
Current will only split equally at a junction if the resistance in each branch is equal.

front: If the potential difference of the power source remains constant, but more components are added to a circuit, what effect does this have on the current?
back: Adding components to a circuit increases the total resistance of the circuit, so the current would decrease (for a constant potential difference).

front: If the potential difference of the power source is increased, but everything else in the circuit remains constant, what effect does this have on the current?
back: If the potential difference of the power source is increased, but everything else in the circuit remains constant, the current will increase.

front: Define electrical power.
back: Electrical power is the rate at which energy is transferred or dissipated by a resistor.

front:
True or False?
Work is done when energy is transferred by moving charges in a circuit.
back:
True.
Work is done when energy is transferred by moving charges in a circuit.

front: How are chemical cells used as an energy source in circuits?
back: Chemical cells use the energy stored in chemicals to arrange charges in a way that produces a potential difference.

front: How are solar cells used as an energy source in circuits?
back: Solar cells use the radiant energy from the Sun to produce a potential difference.

front: How are electrical generators used as a source of electrical energy?
back: Electrical generators use the energy from burning fuels to convert kinetic energy into electric potential energy to produce a potential difference.

front: How are wind generators used as a source of electrical energy?
back: Wind generators use the energy from moving air to convert the kinetic energy of wind into electric potential energy to produce a potential difference.

front: State two advantages of single-use alkaline batteries.
back: Advantages of single-use alkaline batteries are: the chemicals used have a high energy density; they are a convenient source of energy used in everyday appliances; they are a portable source of electrical energy; several batteries can be combined in series to increase p.d.; they are very inexpensive

front: State two disadvantages of single-use alkaline batteries.
back: Disadvantages of single-use alkaline batteries are: they are non-rechargeable and need to be replaced often; they have a high internal resistance; they contribute to pollution when disposed; they are made from non-renewable materials

front: State two advantages of lithium-ion batteries.
back: Advantages of lithium-ion batteries are: they have a very high energy density; they have a high electrical efficiency; they are a convenient source of energy used in everyday appliances (e.g. laptops, phones); they are rechargeable and have a long lifetime; they have a fast charging time; they are a portable source of electrical energy; they have a low internal resistance

front: State two disadvantages of lithium-ion batteries.
back:
Disadvantages of lithium-ion batteries are:
• the charge capacity of the cell degrades over time
• the internal resistance increases over time
• they are expensive compared to other types of battery

front: State two advantages of lead-acid batteries.
back:
Advantages of lead-acid batteries are:
• they are relatively cheap
• they are rechargeable
• they are able to deliver very high currents in a short time which is useful for starting up vehicles

front: State two disadvantages of lead-acid batteries.
back: Disadvantages of lead-acid batteries are: they have a low energy density; the internal resistance increases as the battery degrades over time; they have a limited number of full discharge cycles; they contribute to pollution when disposed as they contain toxic and corrosive materials; they are made from non-renewable materials

front: State two advantages of photovoltaic cells.
back: Advantages of photovoltaic cells are: they provide a virtually unlimited supply of energy; they are a clean energy supply and do not contribute to pollution; the energy source (the Sun) is freely available everywhere; they are cheap to maintain; no input of fuel is required

front: State two disadvantages of photovoltaic cells.
back: Disadvantages of photovoltaic cells are: the output can be variable due to dependence on weather conditions; energy output can be significantly impacted by poor weather; they have a low efficiency; they can only generate energy during daylight hours; each cell only produces a small amount of electricity; solar farms are required for large scale electricity production

front: State two advantages of wind generators.
back: Advantages of wind generators are: they provide a virtually unlimited supply of energy; they are a clean energy supply and do not contribute to pollution; the energy source (the wind) is freely available everywhere; they are cheap to maintain; no input of fuel is required

front: State two disadvantages of wind generators.
back: Disadvantages of wind generators are: the output can be variable due to dependence on weather conditions; energy output can be significantly impacted by lack of wind; they have a low efficiency; they contribute to noise and visual pollution

front: State two advantages of fossil fuel generators.
back: Advantages of fossil fuel generators are: there is already an extensive infrastructure in place; the fuels used have a high energy density; they are highly reliable and provide energy consistently; they are a well-known and developed technology

front: State two disadvantages of fossil fuel generators.
back: Disadvantages of fossil fuel generators are: they produce significant greenhouse gas emissions which contribute to global warming; they produce other polluting gases which contribute to acid rain and other environmental issues; fossil fuels are a non-renewable energy source

front: Define electromotive force (emf).
back: Electromotive force (emf) is the total energy transferred in a source of electrical energy per unit charge passing through it.

front: Define internal resistance.
back: Internal resistance is the resistance of a source of electrical energy, such as batteries, as they are not perfect conductors.

front: Define terminal potential difference.
back: Terminal potential difference is the potential difference across the terminals of a source of electrical energy when it is supplying a current to a circuit.

front: What are ' lost volts '?
back: 'Lost volts' refer to the voltage drop, or decrease in potential difference, that occurs when a source of electrical energy supplies a current to a circuit.

back:

front:
True or False?
When the internal resistance is zero, the terminal p.d. of a cell is less than its emf.
back:
False.
When the internal resistance is zero, the terminal p.d. of a cell is equal to its emf. This is when no current flows.

front:
True or False?
When a current flows, the terminal p.d. of a cell will be less than its emf.
back:
True.
When a current flows, the terminal p.d. of a cell will be less than its emf. This is because there will be a potential drop across the internal resistance.

front: What is a thermistor?
back:
A thermistor is a temperature-dependent resistor.
This means its resistance changes depending on its temperature.

front: How does the resistance of a thermistor change when its temperature is increased?
back: When the temperature of a thermistor is increased, its resistance decreases.

front: What is an LDR?
back:
LDR stands for light-dependent resistor.
This means its resistance changes depending on the intensity of light on it.

front: How does the resistance of an LDR change when the intensity of light on it is increased?
back:
When light intensity on an LDR is increased, its resistance decreases.
(Remember: L ight D ecreases R esistance - LDR)

front: What is a variable resistor?
back:
A variable resistor is a resistor that can change the resistance by changing the length of the wire that makes up the circuit.
This is because a longer length of wire has more resistance than a shorter length of wire.

front: What is a potentiometer?
back: A potentiometer is a type of variable resistor that uses a sliding contact to vary the potential difference in a circuit.

front: How many oscillations are shown by the pendulum in the diagram?
back: The pendulum in the diagram shows one oscillation.

front: What is an oscillation?
back: An oscillation is the repetitive variation with time of the displacement of an object about the equilibrium position ().

front: Define the term equilibrium position in simple harmonic motion.
back: The term equilibrium position in simple harmonic motion is the position where there is no resultant force acting on an object.

front: What does displacement mean in oscillations?
back: Displacement in oscillations is the horizontal or vertical distance of a point on the wave from its equilibrium position.

front:
True or False?
The period of an oscillation is measured in seconds.
back:
True.
The period of an oscillation is measured in seconds (s).

front: What is the amplitude of an oscillation?
back: The amplitude of an oscillation is the maximum value of the displacement on either side of the equilibrium position.

front: State the meaning of frequency in terms of oscillations.
back: Frequency is the number of oscillations per second and it is measured in hertz (Hz).

front: Define angular frequency.
back: Angular frequency is the change of angular displacement with respect to time and is measured in radians per second (rad s⁻¹).

front: What is simple harmonic motion (SHM)?
back: Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is a type of oscillation where the restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement and directed towards the equilibrium position.

front:
True or False?
In SHM, the time interval of each complete vibration is the same.
back:
True.
In SHM, the time interval of each complete vibration, known as the period, is constant.

front: What are the two properties of the restoring force in simple harmonic motion?
back:
The two properties of the restoring force in simple harmonic motion are that:
• it is always directed towards the equilibrium position
• it is proportional to the displacement from the equilibrium position

front: State one example of an object undergoing SHM.
back:
Examples of objects undergoing SHM are:
• The pendulum of a clock
• A child on a swing
• A rope bridge
• A marble in a bowl
• A bowl set vibrating
• A mass oscillating on a spring
• A bungee jumper coming to a stop at the end of their fall

front: How does acceleration relate to displacement in SHM?
back: In SHM, acceleration is proportional to displacement and in the opposite direction to it.

front:

The period of oscillation in SHM depends on the amplitude of oscillation.
back:
False.
The period of oscillation in SHM is independent of the amplitude for small angles of oscillation.

front: Define angular frequency in the context of SHM.
back: Angular frequency in SHM is the change of angular displacement with respect to time, measured in radians per second (rad s⁻¹).

True or False?
The time period of a mass-spring system depends on gravitational field strength.

False.
The time period of a mass-spring system is independent of the gravitational field strength.

front: How does the spring constant, k, affect the time period of a mass-spring system?
back: The higher the spring constant, k, the stiffer the spring and the shorter the time period of the oscillation.

front: What is a simple pendulum?

front: How are waves generated?
back: Waves are generated by oscillating sources.

front: Define the displacement of a wave.
back: The displacement of a wave is the distance of a point on the wave from its equilibrium position.

front: Define the wavelength of a wave.
back: The wavelength of a wave is the length of one complete oscillation measured from the same point on two consecutive waves.

front: Define the amplitude of a wave.
back: The amplitude of a wave is the maximum displacement of an oscillating wave from its equilibrium position.

front: Define the period of a wave.
back: The period of a wave is the time taken for a complete oscillation to pass a fixed point.

front: Define the frequency of a wave.
back: The frequency of a wave is the number of complete oscillations to pass a fixed point per unit time.

front: Define wave speed.
back: Wave speed is the distance travelled by a wave per unit time.

back:

front: Define a transverse wave.
back: A wave is transverse if the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of wave motion and energy transfer.

front: Define a longitudinal wave.
back: A wave is longitudinal if the oscillations are parallel to the direction of wave motion and energy transfer.

front:
True or False?
Longitudinal waves can travel through a vacuum, while transverse waves cannot.
back:
False.
Transverse waves can travel through a vacuum, while longitudinal waves cannot.

front: Define a rarefaction.
back: A rarefaction is an area of low pressure in a longitudinal wave, where the particles are further apart from each other.

front: Define a compression.
back: A compression is an area of high pressure in a longitudinal wave, where the particles are closer together.

front: Give an example of a transverse wave.
back: Examples of transverse waves are: electromagnetic waves; surface water waves; vibrations on a guitar string; seismic S-waves (secondary waves)

front: Give an example of a longitudinal wave.
back: Examples of longitudinal waves are: sound waves; ultrasound; seismic P-waves (primary waves); tsunami wave

front:
True or False?
Soundwaves are transverse waves and need a medium in which to propagate.
back:
False.
Soundwaves are longitudinal waves, but they do need a medium in which to propagate.

front:
True or False?
Infrasound waves are waves with frequencies above the range of human hearing.
back:
False.
Infrasound waves are waves with frequencies below the range of human hearing.

front: State the frequency range of human hearing.
back: The frequency range of human hearing is 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.

front: Define ultrasound.
back: Ultrasound waves are waves with frequencies above the range of human hearing, >20 kHz.

front:
True or False?
Sound waves with higher frequencies have a higher pitch.
back:
True.
Sound waves with higher frequencies have a higher pitch.

front:
True or False?
Sound waves with larger amplitudes have a lower volume.
back:
False.
Sound waves with larger amplitudes have a greater volume.

front:
True or False?
The temperature of the air affects the speed of sound travelling through it.
back:
True.
The temperature of the air affects the speed of sound travelling through it.
The higher the temperature of the air, the faster sound can travel.

front:
True or False?
Sound travels faster in gases than in solids.
back:
False.
Sound travels faster in solids than in gases.
This is because the particles in a solid are closer together, so they can transfer energy through oscillations more quickly than in a gas.

front: How is an electromagnetic wave generated?
back: An electromagnetic wave is generated by the combined oscillation of an electric and a magnetic field.

front:
True or False?
In an electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic fields oscillate parallel to each other.
back:
False.
In an electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic fields oscillate perpendicularly to each other.

front:
True or False?
Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum.
back:
True.
Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum.

front: At what speed does a gamma wave travel through the vacuum of space?
back:
A gamma wave travels through the vacuum of space at the speed of light,

.

front: Which type of electromagnetic radiation has the lowest energy?
back:
The type of electromagnetic radiation with the lowest energy is radio waves.
This is because the lower the frequency of the EM wave, the less energy it transfers. Radio waves have the lowest frequency and therefore the lowest energy.

front: Which electromagnetic waves have a shorter wavelength than ultraviolet waves?
back:
The electromagnetic waves with a shorter wavelength than ultraviolet are:
• x-rays
• gamma rays

front: Which part of the visible spectrum has wavelengths in the region of 700 nm?
back: The part of the visible spectrum which has wavelengths in the region of 700 nm is red light.

front: What is the range of wavelengths that human eyes can detect?
back: The range of wavelengths that human eyes can detect is called the visible spectrum. The visible spectrum has wavelengths between 400 nm and 700 nm.

front: What type of wave requires a medium, and can be either transverse or longitudinal?
back: Mechanical waves require a medium, and can be either transverse or longitudinal.

front: What type of wave does not require a medium, and travels at the speed of light?
back: Electromagnetic waves do not require a medium, and travel at the speed of light.

front: What is a wavefront?
back: A wavefront is a line joining all the points on a wave that oscillate in phase and are perpendicular to the direction of motion.

front: Define a ray in the context of waves.
back: A ray is a line showing the direction of motion and energy transfer of the wave, perpendicular to the wavefront.

front:
True or False?
A surface wave propagates in three dimensions.
back:
False.
A surface wave propagates in two dimensions.

front: What shape do wavefronts have for a surface wave?
back: The wavefronts for a surface wave are circular.

front: How are peaks and troughs represented in wavefront diagrams?
back: Peaks are represented with a darker line and troughs with a fainter line.

front: What is the distance between successive peak wavefronts called?
back: The distance between successive peak wavefronts is called the wavelength.

front: Define circular wavefronts.
back: Circular wavefronts are wavefronts that propagate in two dimensions, such as those on the surface of water.

front: What are spherical wavefronts?
back: Spherical wavefronts are wavefronts that propagate in three dimensions, such as those of sound or light waves.

front: State the relationship between wavefronts and rays.
back: Wavefronts are perpendicular to rays. Rays indicate the direction of motion and energy transfer of the wave.

front: What is the graphical representation of a transverse wave in a horizontal plane?
back: The graphical representation of a transverse wave in a horizontal plane shows wavefronts as parallel vertical lines.

front: Define reflection.
back: Reflection is when a wave hits a boundary between two media and bounces back to the original medium without passing through.

front: State the law of reflection.
back: The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence, , equals the angle of reflection, r.

front:
True or False?
During reflection, the frequency of the wave changes.
back:
False.
During reflection, the frequency, wavelength, and speed of the wave do not change.

front: Define refraction.
back: Refraction is the change in direction of a wave when it passes through a boundary between mediums of different densities.

front: How does wave speed change when passing from a less dense to a more dense medium?
back: When a wave travels from a less dense medium to a more dense medium, its speed decreases.

front: What is the angle of incidence?
back: The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal line at the boundary between two media.

front: What happens to light when it travels from air to glass?
back: When light travels from air to glass, its speed decreases, its wavelength decreases, and it refracts towards the normal.

front:
True or False?
Refraction occurs without transmission when a wave passes through the boundary between two media.
back:
False.
Refraction always involves the transmission of the wave into the second medium.

front: Define transmission.
back: Transmission is when a wave passes through a substance, and refraction is a specific type of transmission involving a change in direction.

front: What happens to the angle of refraction when light travels from a denser to a less dense medium?
back: When light travels from a denser to a less dense medium, the angle of refraction is greater than the angle of incidence, causing the light to bend away from the normal.

Diffraction occurs when waves pass through an aperture.
back:
True.
Diffraction occurs when waves pass through an aperture or around a barrier.

front: What happens to wave amplitude during diffraction through an aperture?
back: Wave amplitude decreases during diffraction through an aperture because the barrier on either side of the gap absorbs wave energy.

front: How does gap size relative to wavelength affect diffraction?
back: Gap size relative to wavelength affects diffraction because diffraction occurs when the gap size is similar to the wavelength. More diffraction occurs if the wavelength is larger than the gap size.

front: What happens when waves pass through a gap much larger than the wavelength?
back: When waves pass through a gap much larger than the wavelength, the majority of the wave passes straight through with little diffraction.

front: Define diffraction around a barrier.
back: Diffraction around a barrier is when waves curve around the edge of the barrier and spread out behind it.

front: What determines the extent of diffraction around a barrier?
back: The extent of diffraction around a barrier is determined by the wavelength of the waves. Longer wavelengths undergo greater diffraction.

front: What is the effect of a barrier larger than the wavelength on the amount of wave diffraction?
back: The effect of a barrier larger than the wavelength is some diffraction occurs and a shadow region forms behind the barrier where no wavefronts are present.

front: How does wavelength compared to barrier size affect diffraction?
back: Wavelength compared to barrier size affects diffraction because if the barrier is the same size as the wavelength, there is more diffraction and a smaller shadow region behind the barrier.

front: What is the relationship between wavelength and optimal diffraction?
back: Optimal diffraction occurs when the wavelength is comparable to the size of the gap or barrier.

front: What is Snell's law?
back: Snell's law relates the angle of incidence to the angle of refraction at a boundary between two media.

front: What is superposition?
back: Superposition is when two or more waves arrive at the same point and their amplitudes combine.

front: Define the principle of superposition.
back: The principle of superposition states that when two or more waves overlap at a point, the displacement at that point is the sum of the displacements of the individual waves.

front:
True or False?
Superposition only applies to transverse waves.
back:
False.
The principle of superposition applies to both transverse and longitudinal waves.

front: What does constructive interference mean?
back: Constructive interference occurs when two or more waves superimpose and have displacements in the same direction.

front: What is destructive interference?
back: Destructive interference occurs when two or more waves superimpose and have displacements in opposite directions.

front: How do waves interfere constructively?
back: Waves interfere constructively when they are in phase and their displacements add together to form a larger displacement.

front: What happens to waves after they undergo superposition?
back: After waves undergo superposition, they continue to travel as normal.

front: State the meaning of resultant displacement.
back: Resultant displacement is the vector sum of the displacements of individual waves when they overlap.

front: What must be constant for a clear interference pattern?
back: For a clear interference pattern, the waves must be of the same type, amplitude, frequency, and have a constant phase difference.

front: When does destructive interference occur?

front: What is a wavefront?
back: A wavefront is a line joining all the points on a wave that oscillate in phase and are perpendicular to the direction of motion.

front: Define a ray in the context of waves.
back: A ray is a line showing the direction of motion and energy transfer of the wave, perpendicular to the wavefront.

front:
True or False?
A surface wave propagates in three dimensions.
back:
False.
A surface wave propagates in two dimensions.

front: What shape do wavefronts have for a surface wave?
back: The wavefronts for a surface wave are circular.

front: How are peaks and troughs represented in wavefront diagrams?
back: Peaks are represented with a darker line and troughs with a fainter line.

front: What is the distance between successive peak wavefronts called?
back: The distance between successive peak wavefronts is called the wavelength.

front: Define circular wavefronts.
back: Circular wavefronts are wavefronts that propagate in two dimensions, such as those on the surface of water.

front: What are spherical wavefronts?
back: Spherical wavefronts are wavefronts that propagate in three dimensions, such as those of sound or light waves.

front: State the relationship between wavefronts and rays.
back: Wavefronts are perpendicular to rays. Rays indicate the direction of motion and energy transfer of the wave.

front: What is the graphical representation of a transverse wave in a horizontal plane?

front: Define reflection.
back: Reflection is when a wave hits a boundary between two media and bounces back to the original medium without passing through.

front: State the law of reflection.
back: The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence, i, equals the angle of reflection, r.

front:
True or False?
During reflection, the frequency of the wave changes.
back:
False.
During reflection, the frequency, wavelength, and speed of the wave do not change.

front: Define refraction.
back: Refraction is the change in direction of a wave when it passes through a boundary between mediums of different densities.

front: How does wave speed change when passing from a less dense to a more dense medium?
back: When a wave travels from a less dense medium to a more dense medium, its speed decreases.

front: What is the angle of incidence?
back: The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal line at the boundary between two media.

front: What happens to light when it travels from air to glass?
back: When light travels from air to glass, its speed decreases, its wavelength decreases, and it refracts towards the normal.

front:

Refraction occurs without transmission when a wave passes through the boundary between two media.
back:
False.
Refraction always involves the transmission of the wave into the second medium.

front: Define transmission.
back: Transmission is when a wave passes through a substance, and refraction is a specific type of transmission involving a change in direction.

front: What happens to the angle of refraction when light travels from a denser to a less dense medium?
back: When light travels from a denser to a less dense medium, the angle of refraction is greater than the angle of incidence, causing the light to bend away from the normal.

back: A single slit diffraction pattern is a series of light and dark fringes produced by monochromatic light passing through a single rectangular slit onto a screen.

front: Define central maximum in a single slit diffraction pattern.
back: The central maximum is the brightest and widest fringe in a single slit diffraction pattern.

The central maximum in a single slit diffraction pattern is wider than the maxima in a double slit diffraction pattern.

front: How does changing the wavelength of the incident light affect the diffraction pattern in a single-slit experiment?
back: Increasing the wavelength of the incident light increases the angle of diffraction, causing wider fringes.

front: What is the effect of increasing the distance between the slit and the screen in a single slit diffraction experiment?

front: Define the term fringe in the context of diffraction patterns.
back: A fringe is a bright or dark band resulting from the constructive or destructive interference of light waves.

front: What is a standing wave?
back: A standing wave is produced by the superposition of two waves traveling in opposite directions with the same frequency.

front:
True or False?
Standing waves transfer energy.
back:
False.
Standing waves store energy. Progressive waves transfer energy.

front: What is the main difference between progressive and standing waves?
back: The main difference is that progressive waves transfer energy, while standing waves store energy.

front: Define a progressive wave.
back: A progressive wave is a wave that transfers energy from one place to another.

front: What conditions must be met for a standing wave to form?
back: For standing waves to form, the waves must have the same wavelength and a similar amplitude.

front:
True or False?
The principle of superposition applies only to transverse waves.
back:
False.
The principle of superposition applies to all types of waves, including transverse, longitudinal, progressive, and stationary waves.

front: What is a node in a standing wave?
back: A node in a standing wave is a location of zero amplitude, where destructive interference occurs.

front: Define an antinode.
back: An antinode is a location of maximum amplitude in a standing wave, where constructive interference occurs.

front:
True or False?
Nodes are locations of maximum amplitude.
back:
False.
Nodes are locations of zero amplitude.

front:
True or False?
Points within a "loop" of a standing wave are in phase.
back:
True.
Points within a "loop" of a standing wave are in phase.

front: What is the phase difference between two points with an odd number of nodes between them?
back: The phase difference between two points with an odd number of nodes between them is π (anti-phase).

front: Explain the difference between phase differences in standing and travelling waves.
back: The phase difference between two points on travelling waves can range from 0 to 2π, while in standing waves, they can only be 0 (in-phase) or π (anti-phase).

front: What does boundary condition mean in the context of standing waves?
back: Boundary condition refers to whether the ends of the medium (string or pipe) are fixed or free.

front: How do boundary conditions affect the formation of standing waves?
back: Boundary conditions affect the formation of standing waves because they determine the positions of nodes and antinodes and the possible standing wave patterns.

front: Define natural frequency.
back: Natural frequency is the specific frequency at which an integer number of half wavelengths fit on the length of the string or pipe.

front: What is the effect of tension on the frequency of a vibrating string?
back: The frequency of a vibrating string increases with increasing tension.

front: Which boundary conditions can exist for a pipe?

• closed at both ends
• open at both ends
• closed at one end and open at the other

front: What is the meaning of a fixed end in a standing wave?

front:
True or False?
The reflected wave at a free end of a standing wave is in phase with the incident wave.

True.
The reflected wave at the free end of a standing wave is in phase with the incident wave.

front: What is a forced oscillation?

front: What factors must be considered to provide enough energy to a satellite to put it into orbit?

• the satellite must overcome frictional forces
• additional energy must be allowed for thermal energy dissipation

front: What happens to the orbital speed of a satellite in a circular orbit as its orbit becomes lower due to drag?

front: Define 1 coulomb (C).

front:

front: How is this carbon atom electrically neutral?
back:
The carbon atom contains:
• 6 positive protons
• 6 negative electrons
• 6 neutral neutrons
The amount of positive and negative charge is equal, so the carbon atom is electrically neutral.

front: How is charge quantised?
back: Charge is quantised because any quantity of charge will always equal a whole number of protons or electrons, which have a charge equal to ±1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

front: Is the electric force between two charges of the same type attractive or repulsive?
back: The electric force on two charges of the same type is repulsive (directed away from each other).

front: Is the electric force between two opposite charges attractive or repulsive?
back: The electric force on two opposite charges is attractive (directed towards each other).

front: What is the law of conservation of charge?
back: The law of conservation of charge states that the total charge in an isolated system remains constant.

When two charged spheres come into contact, the charges are shared between them until they are evenly distributed.
back:
True.
When two charged spheres come into contact, the charges are shared between them until they are evenly distributed. As a result, both spheres will have an equal charge.

front: What is charging by friction?
back:
Charging by friction is the transfer of charge (electrons) when two insulating substances move past one another.
One substance gains an excess of positive charge and the other gains an excess of negative charge.

front: What is charging by contact?
back:
Charging by contact is the transfer of charge (electrons) between two substances when there is physical contact between them.
The excess, or deficit, of electrons, is shared between the two substances.

front: What is charging by induction?
back:
Charging by induction is the separation of charge caused by the influence of a nearby charged object without any physical contact.
The charged object causes electrons near the surface of the uncharged substance to be either repelled or attracted.

front: Describe the movement of electrons when an uncharged acetate rod is rubbed with an uncharged cloth.
back: When an uncharged acetate rod is rubbed with an uncharged cloth: electrons are transferred from the acetate rod to the cloth by friction; the cloth becomes negatively charged because it gains electrons; the acetate rod becomes positively charged because it loses electrons

False.

A metal sphere can become positively charged by induction by using a positively charged rod.

False.

When inducing a charge on a metal sphere, its final charge will always be opposite to the rod.

front: How can a metal sphere become charged by contact?
back:

• bringing a charged rod into contact with the sphere (this allows electrons to flow to or from the sphere)
• removing the rod (this leaves an excess charge)

• the cloth becomes negatively charged because it gains electrons
• the acetate rod becomes positively charged because it loses electrons

front:
True or False?
Earthing a charged body causes it to discharge until its potential drops to half its initial value.
back:
False.
Earthing a charged body causes it to discharge until it has a potential of 0 V.

front: How can a metal sphere become charged by induction?
back:
A metal sphere can become charged by induction by
• bringing a charged rod near the sphere without touching it (this separates the charges)
• earthing the sphere (this allows electrons to flow to or from the sphere)
• removing the earth connection and the rod (this leaves an excess charge)

front:
True or False?
A metal sphere can become positively charged by induction by using a positively charged rod.
back:
False.
A metal sphere can become positively charged by induction by using a negatively charged rod.
When inducing a charge on a metal sphere, its final charge will always be opposite to the rod.

front: How can a metal sphere become charged by contact?
back:
A metal sphere can become charged by contact by
• bringing a charged rod into contact with the sphere (this allows electrons to flow to or from the sphere)
• removing the rod (this leaves an excess charge)

front: How can sparks occur when refuelling an aircraft?
back:
Sparks can occur when
• there is a large build-up of charge on the aircraft
• the potential difference becomes large enough for current to travel through the air

front: How can the risk of sparks be reduced when refuelling an aircraft?
back: When refuelling an aircraft, the risk of sparking can be reduced by earthing the aircraft and fuel tank to carry excess charge away.

front: Define electric field strength at a point.
back: The electric field strength at a point is the force per unit charge experienced by a small positive test charge placed at that point.

front: What are the two equivalent units of electric field strength?
back: The two equivalent units of electric field strength are N C-1 and V m-1.

front: What is the significance of a test charge?
back:
Test charges are used to define the strength of a field at a point and the direction a charge will movein the field.
This is because electric field strength is a vector quantity.

front: How is the direction of an electric field defined?
back:
The direction of an electric field is defined by the direction of the force that acts on a positive test charge, such that
• the force on a positive charge is in the direction of the field
• the force on a negative charge is in the opposite direction

Inside the charged sphere, the electric field strength is zero.

back:
The resultant electric field due to multiple charges is determined by vector addition. This could be
• using simple addition (if the point lies on a line joining the charges)
• using Pythagoras (if the point makes a right-angled triangle with the charges)

front: How is a uniform electric field set up?

The field lines around the edges of two parallel plates are uniform.

front: What is the relationship between electric field strength and line density?

The density of field lines represents the strength of an electric field
• the closer together the field lines, the stronger the field

front: Define electric potential at a point.
back: The electric potential at a point is the work done per unit charge in taking a small positive test charge from infinity to a defined point.

front:

Electric potential is a vector quantity.
back:
False.
Electric potential is a scalar quantity.

front: What is the unit of electric potential?
back: The unit of electric potential is J C-1 or V.

back: For a positive charge, electric potential decreases as the distance increases.

Electric potential increases in the direction of electric field lines.

False.
Electric potential decreases in the direction of electric field lines.

front:
True or False?
Inside a charged sphere, the electric potential is zero.

False.

front:
True or False?
The combined electric potential at a point due to multiple charges is determined by vector addition.
back:
False.
The combined electric potential at a point due to multiple charges is determined by adding together the potentials due to each of the charges.

front: Define electric potential energy.
back: Electric potential energy is the work done when bringing all the charges in a systemto their positions from infinity.

front:
True or False?
Electric potential energy is always positive.
back:
False.
Electric potential energy can be positive or negative depending on the signs of the charges involved.

front: What happens to the electric potential energy of two similar charges as their separation increases?
back: The electric potential energy of two similar charges decreases as the separation between them increases.

front: What happens to the electric potential energy of two opposite charges as their separation increases?

True.

front: What does the area under a force-distance graph represent?
back: The area under a force-distance graph represents the change in electric potential energy or the work done in moving the charge from one point to another.

When a small mass moves away from a large mass, the gravitational potential energy increases.
The change in electric potential energy is similar when:
• a small positive charge moves away from a large negative charge
• a small positive charge moves towards a large positive charge

front: Name two scenarios in which the change in electric potential energy is similar to the change in gravitational potential when a small mass moves towards a large mass.
back:
When a small mass moves towards a large mass, the gravitational potential energy decreases.
The change in electric potential energy is similar when:
• a small positive charge moves towards a large negative charge
• a small positive charge moves away from a large positive charge

back: Potential gradient is the rate of change of electric potential with respect to displacement in the direction of the field.

front: What does the gradient of a V − r graph represent?
back: The gradient of a potential-distance (V − r) graph represents the electric field strength at that point.

back: The area under a field-distance (E − r) graph represents the potential difference between the two points.

True or False?
The V − r graph for a positive charge follows a −1/r relation

True or False?
The E − r graph for a negative charge follows a −1/r relation
back:
False.
The field-distance (E − r) graph for a negative charge follows a −1/r2 (inverse square law) relation.
All values of field strength are negative for a negative charge

front:
True or False?
The curve of an E − r graph is steeper than its corresponding V − r graph
back:
True.
The curve of an E − r graph is steeper than its corresponding V − r graph.
This is because E − r graphs follow a 1/r2 relation whereas V − r graphs follow a 1/r relation.

front: What is an electric equipotential surface?
back: Equipotential surfaces (or lines) connect points of equal electric potential.

front:
True or False?
Equipotential lines are always parallel to electric field lines.
back:
False.
Equipotential lines are always perpendicular to electric field lines.

front:
True or False?
No work is done as a charge moves along an equipotential line.
back:
True.
No work is done as a charge moves along an equipotential line.

front: What are the key features of the equipotential lines in a radial electric field?
back:
The key features of the equipotential lines in a radial electric field are:
• concentric circles
• become further apart with distance

front: What are the key features of the equipotential lines in a uniform electric field?
back:
The key features of the equipotential lines in a uniform electric field are:
• horizontal straight lines
• parallel
• equally spaced

front: Define magnetic flux density.
back: The magnetic flux density of a field is the number of magnetic field lines passing through a region of space per unit area.

back: One tesla (T) is the flux density that causes a force of 1 N on a1 m wire carrying a current of 1 A at right angles to the field.

front: What is the relationship between flux density and the strength of a magnetic field?
back:
The flux density is a measure of the strength of a magnetic field
• the higher the flux density, the stronger the magnetic field
• the lower the flux density, the weaker the magnetic field

front: How is a uniform magnetic field set up?
back: A uniform magnetic field can be set up between two flat permanent magnets when the north pole of one magnet is parallel to the south pole of the other.

front: What is the right-hand grip rule?

The right-hand grip rule is used to determine the direction of a magnetic field around a current:

Fleming's left-hand rule is used to determine the direction of the magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire.

front: What three factors affect the amount of deflection of a charged particle in a uniform electric field?

The amount of deflection of a charged particle in a magnetic field depends on:

• the magnitude of the charge of the particle
• the speed of the particle

A heavier particle will deflect more than a lighter particle with the same charge.

The greater the mass, the smaller the deflection. Therefore, a heavier particle will deflect less than a lighter particle with the same charge.

True.

This means it travels a smaller horizontal distance before hitting the plate.

front:
True or False?
A fast-moving electron will deflect less than a slow-moving electron.
back:
True.
The greater the speed, the smaller the deflection. Therefore, a fast-moving electron will deflect less than a slow-moving electron.
This means it travels a greater horizontal distance before hitting the plate.

front: How can a charged particle moving at a constant speed in perpendicularly orientated uniform electric and magnetic fields continue to move in a straight line?
back: A charged particle will continue to move at a constant speed in a straight line if the electric and magnetic forces acting on it are equal and opposite.

front: Define electromagnetic induction.
back: Electromagnetic induction is the process in which an e.m.f or current is induced in a closed circuit due to changes in magnetic flux.

For electromagnetic induction to occur there must be relative motion between a conductor and a magnetic field.

True.

This could be achieved by, for example, moving a conductor through a magnetic field, or moving a magnet through a coil.

front: Define induced e.m.f. in a conductor.
back: The induced e.m.f. in a conductor is the amount of work done per unit charge in separating the charges to the ends of the conductor.

front: How is an e.m.f. induced when a conductor cuts through magnetic field lines?
back:
When a conductor cuts through magnetic field lines, an e.m.f. is induced as:
• free electrons (in the conductor) experience a magnetic force
• the magnetic force causes charges to separate
• the charge separation produces a potential difference (e.m.f.) across the ends of the conductor

An e.m.f. can be induced in a conductor without connecting it to a circuit.
back:
True.
An e.m.f. can be induced in a conductor without connecting it to a circuit.
However, an induced current will only flow if the conductor is connected to a closed circuit.

The magnitude of an induced e.m.f. can be increased by
• increasing the length of the conductor in the field
• increasing the magnetic field strength
• increasing the velocity of the conductor
• increasing the number of turns of wire

front: Define magnetic flux.
back:
Magnetic flux is the product of magnetic flux density and the area perpendicular to the field lines.
It is a measure of the number of field lines in a given area.

The sides of the coil cut the field lines at the fastest rate at this position.

Faraday's Law applies only to coils of wire.

front: State Lenz's Law.
back: Lenz's law states the induced e.m.f in a coil or wire is such that it will oppose the change causing it.

front:
What does the negative sign represent in the equation

?

front:
True or False?
Lenz's Law is a consequence of the principle of conservation of energy.
back:

Lenz's Law is a consequence of the principle of conservation of energy.

front: What happens to the direction of induced current when the direction of a magnet's motion is reversed?
back: When the direction of a magnet's motion is reversed, the direction of the induced current is also reversed.

front: What is self-induction?
back: Self-induction is the effect in which a change in the current tends to produce an induced e.m.f. which opposes the change of current in the same circuit

front: What is mutual induction?
back: Mutual induction is the effect in which a change in the current in one circuit tends to produce an induced e.m.f. which opposes the change of current in a neighbouring circuit

front:
True or False?
The back e.m.f. in self-induction is directly proportional to the rate of current change.
back:
False.
The back e.m.f. in self-induction is proportional to minus the rate of current change

front: What is a transformer?
back: A transformer is a device that changes high alternating voltage at low current to low alternating voltage at high current, and vice versa.

front: What is the role of the soft iron core in a transformer?
back: The role of the soft iron core in a transformer is to significantly increase the strength of the magnetic field from the primary to the secondary coil.

front:
True or False?
In a step-up transformer, the primary coil has more turns than the secondary coil.
back:
False.
In a step-up transformer, the secondary coil has more turns than the primary coil

front: What is an A.C. generator?
back:
An A.C. generator is a device which converts energy from a mechanical store to an electrical store.
The output of an A.C. generator is alternating current.

front: What components make up a simple A.C. generator?
back:
A simple A.C. generator consists of the following components:
• a rectangular coil of wire rotating in a magnetic field
• slip rings and brushes

front: What is the purpose of slip rings in an A.C. generator?
back: The purpose of slip rings in an A.C. generator is to provide a continuous connection between the rotating coil and the external circuit.

In an A.C. generator, the maximum e.m.f is induced when the magnetic flux linkage through the coil is at a maximum.

front: How can the size of the induced e.m.f. in a rotating coil be increased?

front: What apparatus was used in Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment?
back: The apparatus used in Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment was: a source of alpha particles in a lead container; a thin sheet of gold foil; a movable detector; an evacuated chamber

front: What was the purpose of the lead container in Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment?
back: The purpose of the lead container was to produce a collimated (parallel) beam of alpha particles.

front: Why were gold atoms chosen as the target in Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment?
back:
Gold atoms were chosen as the target in Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment because:
• alpha particles must interact with as few atoms as possible
• gold is very malleable and can be made into a very thin foil

front: Why was the apparatus placed in an evacuated chamber?
back: The apparatus was placed in an evacuated chamber to prevent the alpha particles from being scattered by molecules of air.

front: What were the three main observations from Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment?
back: The three main observations from Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment were: Most alpha particles experienced no deflection; Some alpha particles experienced slight deflections (angles <10°); A tiny number of alpha particles experienced large deflections (angles >90°)

front: What does the observation that most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil in Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment suggest about the structure of the atom?
back: The observation that most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil suggests that the atom is mostly empty space.

front: What does the observation that some alpha particles deflect by small angles in Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment suggest about the structure of the atom?
back: The observation that some alpha particles deflect by small angles in Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment suggests the atom must contain a small, positive charge.

front: What does the observation that a tiny number of alpha particles deflect by large angles in Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment suggest about the structure of the atom?
back: The observation that a tiny number of alpha particles deflect by large angles suggests the majority of the mass and all of the positive charge must be concentrated in a nucleus at the centre of the atom.

front: What are the three subatomic particles that make up an atom?
back:
The three subatomic particles that make up an atom are:
• protons (in the nucleus)
• neutrons (in the nucleus)
• electrons (around the nucleus)

front:
True or False?
The mass of a proton is exactly equal to the mass of a neutron.
back:
False.
While close, the mass of a proton (1.007276 u) is slightly less than the mass of a neutron (1.008665 u).

front: What is meant by the term proton number?
back: The proton number of an atom is the number of protons in its nucleus. This number defines the chemical element.

front: What is meant by the term mass number?
back: The mass number of an atom is the total number of protons and neutrons in its nucleus.

front:
True or False?
The periodic table is ordered by mass number.
back:
False.
The periodic table is ordered by proton number, not mass number.

front: What is the relative charge of an electron?
back: The relative charge of an electron is-1e, where e is the elementary charge.

front:
True or False?
Electrons make up most of the mass of an atom.
back:
False.
Most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus. Electrons have a negligible mass compared to the mass of protons and neutrons.

front: How can the notation below be used to determine the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in atom X?
back:
In nuclear notation: X represents the chemical symbol; A represents the mass number (number of protons and neutrons); Z represents the atomic number (number of protons)
Therefore, Z = number of protons = number of electrons, and A - Z = number of neutrons.

front: What is the mass number and proton number of carbon?
back:
The mass number (top number) of carbon is 12.
The proton number (bottom number) of carbon is 6.

front: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in an atom of beryllium?
back:
The mass number (top number) of beryllium is 9.
The proton number (bottom number) of beryllium is 4.
Therefore, an atom of beryllium contains 4 protons, 5 neutrons and 4 electrons.

front: What is an emission spectrum?
back:
An emission spectrum is a set of discrete wavelengths represented by bright lines on a black background.
These lines represent the photons emitted when electrons in excited atoms transition from higher to lower energy levels.

front: What is an absorption spectrum?
back:
An absorption spectrum is a set of discrete wavelengths represented by dark lines across a continuous spectrum.
These lines represent the photons absorbed when white light passes through a low-pressure gas.

front:
True or False?
Emission and absorption spectra for the same element have lines at different wavelengths.
back:
False.
Emission and absorption spectra for the same element have lines at the same wavelengths.

front: What do atomic spectra provide evidence for?
back: Atomic spectra provide evidence that electrons in atoms can only transition between discrete energy levels.

front: What is the main difference between emission and absorption spectra?
back: The main difference between emission and absorption spectra is that emission spectra appear as bright lines on a dark background, whilst absorption spectra appear as dark lines on a bright, continuous background.

front:
True or False?
Each element produces a unique pattern of spectral lines.
back:
True.
Each element produces a unique pattern of spectral lines, which can be used to identify the element.

back: Ionisation energy is the minimum energy required to remove an electron from the ground state of an atom.

front: What happens to an atom when it absorbs a photon?
back:
When an atom absorbs a photon, an electron moves to a higher energy level.
The atom is said to be in an excited state.

The ground state is the highest possible energy state of an atom.

front: What is the significance of the point of closest approach in the Rutherford alpha scattering experiment?
back: The point of closest approach is the point where the alpha particle's kinetic energy is fully converted to electric potential energy, momentarily stopping the particle before it is repelled.

front: What do the deviations from Rutherford's predictions in the alpha scattering provide evidence for?
back: The deviations from Rutherford's predictions in the alpha scattering experiment provide evidence for the existence of the strong nuclear force.

front:
True or False?
Rutherford's original alpha scattering model accounted for the strong nuclear force.
back:
False.
Rutherford's original alpha scattering model only accounted for electrostatic repulsion and did not include the strong nuclear force.

front: What is observed to happen to the number of back-scattered alpha particles at very high energies in Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment?
back: At very high energies, the number of back-scattered alpha particles in Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment sharply decreases to zero, deviating from Rutherford's predictions.

front: What causes deviations from Rutherford's predications in the alpha scattering experiment?
back: At high energies, the alpha particles become close enough to the nucleus that the strong nuclear force has a greater influence than electric repulsion, which creates deviations in the electrostatic repulsion pattern.

front: How does the atomic number of the target nucleus affect deviations from Rutherford's predictions of his alpha scattering experiment?
back: The atomic number of the target nucleus affects deviations from Rutherford's predictions of his alpha scattering experiment because nuclei with lower atomic numbers show greater deviations at lower energies compared to nuclei with higher atomic numbers.

front: Outline the Bohr model.
back:
The Bohr model states that electrons can only exist in certain stable orbits defined by their angular momentum.
Electrons can only move to a larger or smaller orbit by absorbing or emitting a photon of light.

The Bohr model is compatible with the predictions of classical physics.

front: What is the photoelectric effect?
back: The photoelectric effect is a phenomenon in which electrons are emitted from the surface of a metal upon the absorption of electromagnetic radiation.

front: What are photoelectrons?
back: Photoelectrons are electrons that are emitted from the surface of a metal upon the absorption of electromagnetic radiation.

front:
True or False?
In the photoelectric effect, each electron in the metal can absorb multiple photons.
back:
False.
In the photoelectric effect, each electron in the metal can absorb only one photon.

front: Define threshold frequency.
back: Threshold frequency is the minimum frequency of incident electromagnetic radiation required to remove a photoelectron from the surface of a metal.

front:
True or False?
The threshold frequency is different for different metals.
back:
True.
The threshold frequency is different for different metals.

front: Define work function.
back: The work function is the minimum energy required to release a photoelectron from the surface of a metal.

front:
True or False?
An electron can only escape from the surface of the metal if it absorbs a photon with an energy equal to or higher than the work function.
back:
True.
An electron can only escape from the surface of the metal if it absorbs a photon with an energy equal to or higher than the work function.

front:
True or False?
The work function is different for different metals.
back:
True.
The work function is different for different metals.

front: State the symbol for work function.
back: The symbol for work function is the Greek letter, phi,  Φ .

front:
True or False?
A photon with a frequency greater than the threshold frequency of a metal will also have an energy greater than the work function of the metal.
back:
True.
A photon with a frequency greater than the threshold frequency of a metal will also have an energy greater than the work function of the metal.
This is because the energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency.

front: If a photon has an energy greater than the work function of the metal, what happens to the surplus energy?
back: When a photon has an energy greater than the work function of the metal, a photoelectron is released from the metal and the surplus energy is transferred to the kinetic energy of the photoelectron.

A photon with a frequency equal to the threshold frequency will be able to liberate an electron from the surface of the metal, but that photoelectron will have a kinetic energy of zero.

front:
True or False?
The maximum kinetic energy of a photoelectron is independent of the intensity of the radiation.
back:
True.
The maximum kinetic energy of a photoelectron is independent of the intensity of the radiation.

front:
True or False?
The maximum kinetic energy of a photoelectron is independent of the frequency of the incident photon.
back:
False.
The maximum kinetic energy of a photoelectron depends only on the frequency of the incident photon.
