front: Why is the kinetic energy of a photoelectron independent of the intensity of the incident radiation?
back: The kinetic energy of a photoelectron is independent of the intensity of the incident radiation because each electron can only absorb one photon.

front: Why does the kinetic energy of the photoelectrons vary for a specific metal?
back:
The kinetic energy of the photoelectrons varies because some of the electrons are closer to the surface of the metal than others.
Those that are closer to the surface require less energy to escape and therefore have more surplus energy left over from the photon.

front: Define photoelectric current.
back: The photoelectric current is a measure of the number of photoelectrons emitted per second from the surface of a metal undergoing the photoelectric effect.

front:
True or False?
Photoelectric current is proportional to the intensity of the incident radiation.
back:
True.
Photoelectric current is proportional to the intensity of the incident radiation.

front: Define stopping potential in relation to the photoelectric effect.
back: Stopping potential is the potential difference required to stop photoelectron emission from occurring.

front: What information does the stopping potential provide about the photoelectrons?
back: The stopping potential provides information about the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.

front: What quantum effect can a gold leaf electroscope be used to demonstrate?
back: A gold leaf electroscope can be used to demonstrate the photoelectric effect.

front: How is a gold leaf electroscope used to show the photoelectric effect?
back:
To show the photoelectric effect using a gold leaf electroscope:
• the metal plate is given a negative charge
• the gold leaf is repelled
• UV light is shone onto the metal plate
• photoelectrons are emitted
• the gold leaf is no longer repelled

front:
True or False?
In the gold leaf electroscope demonstration, the gold leaf begins to fall down instantly when illuminated with UV light.
back:
True.
In the gold leaf electroscope demonstration, the gold leaf begins to fall down instantly when illuminated with UV light. This is evidence for the one-to-one quantised transfer of energy from photon to electron.

front:
True or False?
In the gold leaf electroscope demonstration, the gold leaf takes longer to fall at low intensities of UV light and does not happen instantly.
back:
False.
In the gold leaf electroscope demonstration, the gold leaf does take longer to fall at low intensities of UV light, but it does still happen instantly.

front:
True or False?
In the gold leaf electroscope demonstration, the gold leaf does not fall down when lower frequencies of light are used.
back:
True.
In the gold leaf electroscope demonstration, the gold leaf does not fall down when lower frequencies of light are used.
This provides evidence for the threshold frequency and work function of metals.

front:
True or False?
In the gold leaf electroscope demonstration, the gold leaf falls when the intensity of the light is increased, even if the frequency is lower than the threshold frequency.
back:
False.
In the gold leaf electroscope demonstration, the gold leaf does not fall when the intensity of the light is increased if the frequency is lower than the threshold frequency.
This provides evidence for the threshold frequency and work function.

front:
True or False?
Wave theory can be used to explain the photoelectric effect.
back:
False.
Wave theory cannot be used to explain the photoelectric effect; the wave model predicts that:
• photoelectrons would be released at any frequency because energy would be accumulated by the electron with each wavefront
• the kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons should be dependent on the intensity because, for a given frequency, the energy of a wave is proportional to the intensity of the light

front:
True or False?
Louis de Broglie proposed that electrons could behave like waves.
back:
True.
Louis de Broglie proposed that electrons could behave like waves, based on the idea that waves (light) can behave like particles (photons).

front: What is meant by de Broglie wavelength?
back: The de Broglie wavelength is the wavelength associated with a moving particle.

front:

For everyday objects travelling at normal speeds, the de Broglie wavelength is far too small for any quantum effects to be observed.

True or False?
The quantum effects of electron diffraction will only be observable when the width of the aperture is of a similar size to the de Broglie wavelength.
back:
True.
The quantum effects of electron diffraction will only be observable when the width of the aperture is of a similar size to the de Broglie wavelength.

front: What type of atomic lattice is usually used to demonstrate electron diffraction?
back: The type of atomic lattice usually used to demonstrate electron diffraction is graphite film because of its crystalline structure.

front: Describe the diffraction pattern produced from electron diffraction.
back: The diffraction pattern produced from electron diffraction is a series of concentric rings.

front: Explain why the radius of the electron diffraction pattern decreases as the voltage applied to the electron diffraction tube is increased.
back:
As the voltage applied to the electron diffraction tube is increased:
• the speed of the electrons increases
• the momentum of the electrons increases
• the kinetic energy of the electrons increases
• the de Broglie wavelength decreases
• the angle of diffraction decreases
• therefore, the radius of the diffraction pattern decreases

front: What is meant by wave-particle duality?
back: Wave-particle duality is the theory that light can behave as a particle and as a wave.

front: Give one experiment that provides evidence that light behaves like a wave, and one that provides evidence that light behaves like a particle.
back:
One experiment that provides evidence that light behaves like a wave is Young's double slit experiment.
One experiment that provides evidence that light behaves like a particle is the photoelectric effect.

front: Which scientist proposed the corpuscular theory of light, that first described light as particle-like in 1672?
back: Newton proposed the corpuscular theory of light in 1672, which first described light as particle-like.

front: Which scientist proposed the wavelet theory of light that first described light as a wave in 1690?
back: Huygens proposed the wavelet theory of light in 1690, which first described light as a wave.

front: Which scientist proved that light has wave-like behaviour in 1803 with his double slit diffraction experiment?
back: Young proved that light has wave-like behaviour in 1803 with his double slit diffraction experiment.

front: Which scientist first observed the photoelectric effect in 1887, proving that light also has particle-like behaviour?
back: Hertz first observed the photoelectric effect in 1887, proving that light also has particle-like behaviour.

front: Which scientist first proposed the idea of quantised energy around 1900?
back: Planck first proposed the idea of quantised energy around 1900 when he identified the Planck constant.

front: Which scientist proposed that light can be described as discrete quanta of energy that behaves like particles in 1905?
back: Einstein proposed that light can be described as discrete quanta of energy that behaves like particles in 1905.

front: Which scientist proposed wave-particle duality in 1924 and theorised the existence of matter waves?
back: De Broglie proposed wave-particle duality in 1924 and theorised the de Broglie wavelength.

front: What is the Compton effect?
back: The Compton effect is the interaction of a high-energy photon with an orbital electron, which causes an increase in the wavelength of the photon and the ejection of the electron.

front: What does Compton scattering provide evidence for?
back: Compton scattering provides evidence for the particle nature of light.

front:
True or False?
Compton scattering can be explained by considering the incident X-rays as waves.
back:
False.
Compton scattering cannot be explained by considering the incident X-rays as waves. It can only be explained using a particle model.

front: Describe the process of Compton scattering.
back:
In Compton scattering:
• a photon collides with an orbital electron and transfers some of its energy
• the wavelength of the photon increases because its energy decreases
• the photon is deflected from its initial path
• the electron is ejected from the atom

front:
True or False?
In Compton scattering, the electron and photon are deflected in the same direction due to conservation of momentum.
back:
False.
In Compton scattering, the electron and photon are deflected in different directions due to conservation of momentum.

front: Define the term isotope.
back: Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons.

front:
True or False?
An element can have only one isotope.
back:
False.
An element can have any number of isotopes, as long as they each have the same number of protons.

front:
True or False?
Two different isotopes of uranium have the same number of neutrons.
back:
False.
Two different isotopes of uranium have the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons.

front:
True or False?
The following atoms are all possible isotopes of chlorine (symbol Cl):
³⁵₁₇Cl, ³⁵₁₈Cl, ³⁵₁₉Cl, ³⁵₂₀Cl
back:
False.
The atoms ³⁵₁₇Cl, ³⁵₁₈Cl, ³⁵₁₉Cl, ³⁵₂₀Cl are not possible isotopes of chlorine as they have the same mass number but different atomic numbers.
Isotopes of an element must have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.

front:
True or False?
The following atoms are all possible isotopes of iron (symbol Fe):
, , ,
back:
True.
The atoms , , ,  are all possible isotopes of iron as they have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.

front: What is isotopic data?
back: Isotopic data refers to the relative amounts of different isotopes of an element present within a substance.

front: Define radioactive decay.
back: Radioactive decay is the random and spontaneous disintegration of an unstable nucleus by emitting alpha, beta, or gamma radiation.

front: How is radioactive decay a random process?
back: Radioactive decay is a random process because the exact time a nucleus will decay cannot be predicted.

front: How is radioactive decay a spontaneous process?
back: Radioactive decay is a spontaneous process because the rate of decay is unaffected by external factors (such as temperature, pressure or chemical conditions).

front:
True or False?
The rate of decay of a sample of radioactive material can be increased by increasing the temperature and pressure of the surroundings.
back:
False.
The rate of decay of a sample of radioactive material cannot be influenced by external factors such as temperature or pressure.

front: Define background radiation.
back: Background radiation is the ionizing radiation that exists around us all the time.

front:
True or False?
Background radiation is solely a human-made phenomenon.
back:
False.
Background radiation is a natural phenomenon that has always existed on Earth and in outer space.

front: Name three natural sources of background radiation.
back: Natural sources of background radiation include: radon gas; cosmic rays from space; radioactive elements in rocks and soil; carbon-14 in living tissue; some food and drink

front: Name three artificial sources of background radiation
back: Artificial sources of background radiation include: nuclear medicine; nuclear waste; nuclear fallout; nuclear accidents

front: How is the count rate of a radioactive source measured?
back: The count rate of a radioactive source is measured using a GM (Geiger-Marsden) tube connected to a counter, or ratemeter.

front: How is the background count accounted for when measuring the count rate of a radioactive source?
back: When measuring the count rate of a radioactive source, the background count is accounted for by measuring the count rate without the source present (background count); measuring the count rate with the source present; subtracting the background count from each measurement of count rate

front: Why it is better to use larger count rates in radioactivity experiments?
back:
It is better to use larger count rates in radioactivity experiments as the background count will be a smaller percentage of the overall count.
As a result, the random variation in each measurement is reduced.

front:
True or False?
Accounting for background count improves the precision of readings.
back:
False.
Accounting for background count improves the accuracy of readings.
This is because background count is a form of systematic error (zero error).

front: Why do some nuclei emit radiation?
back:
Nuclei emit radiation when they are unstable due to having
• an imbalance of protons or neutrons
• an excess amount of energy

front:
True or False?
The composition of a nucleus changes following alpha, beta and gamma decay.
back:
False.
The composition of a nucleus changes following alpha and beta decay, but not following gamma decay.

front: What effect does alpha decay have on a nucleus?
back:
An alpha particle is a helium nucleus:
When a nucleus emits an alpha particle, the effect is:
• nucleon number decreases by 4
• proton number decreases by 2

front: What effect does beta-minus decay have on a nucleus?
back:
A beta-minus particle is an electron:
When a nucleus emits a beta-minus particle, the effect is:
• nucleon number stays the same
• proton number increases by 1

front: What effect does beta-plus decay have on a nucleus?
back:
A beta-plus particle is a positron:
When a nucleus emits a beta-plus particle, the effect is:
• nucleon number stays the same
• proton number decreases by 1

front: What effect does gamma decay have on a nucleus?
back:
Gamma radiation is electromagnetic radiation:
When a nucleus emits gamma radiation, the effect is:
• nucleon number stays the same
• proton number stays the same

front: List the three types of nuclear radiation in order of increasing ionising power.
back:
The types of nuclear radiation in order of increasing ionising power are:
• gamma (least ionising, creates fewest ion pairs per cm)
• beta (creates a moderate amount of ion pairs per cm)
• alpha (most ionising, creates most ion pairs per cm)

front: List the three types of nuclear radiation in order of increasing penetrating power.
back:
The types of nuclear radiation in order of increasing penetrating power are:
• alpha (least penetrating, can be stopped by paper)
• beta (can stopped by a few mm of aluminium)
• gamma (most penetrating, can be reduced by a few mm of lead)

front: Why are beta particles affected more than alpha particles when they pass through the same electric field?
back: In the same electric field, E, the force, F, on a beta particle will be slightly less due to having a smaller charge, q, but it will have a much greater acceleration, a, due to having a smaller mass, m electric force: F = Eq; acceleration: a = F/m

front: Why are beta particles affected more than alpha particles when they pass through the same magnetic field?
back: In the same perpendicular magnetic field, B, the force, F, on a beta particle will generally be higher as, despite having a smaller charge, q, it will typically travel at a much greater speed, v. It also has a greater acceleration, a, due to having a smaller mass, m magnetic force: F = qvB; acceleration: a = F/m

front:
True or False?
Electron anti-neutrinos are emitted during beta-plus decay.
back:
False.
Electron anti-neutrinos are emitted during beta-minus decay.
Beta-minus decay is when a neutron turns into a proton and emits a beta-minus particle and an electron anti-neutrino.

front:
True or False?
An electron neutrino is emitted when a proton turns into a neutron.
back:
True.
An electron neutrino is emitted along with a beta-plus particle when a proton turns into a neutron.

front:
True or False?
Nuclei with too many neutrons decay by either beta-minus decay or beta-plus decay.
back:
False.
Nuclei with too many neutrons decay by beta-minus decay only.

front:
True or False?
Nuclei with too many protons decay by either beta-plus decay or electron capture.
back:
True.
Nuclei with too many protons decay by either beta-plus decay or electron capture.

front:
True or False?
Alpha decay usually occurs in small unstable nuclei.
back:
False.
Nuclei with too many nucleons (protons and neutrons) decay by alpha decay.
Therefore, alpha decay usually occurs in very large unstable nuclei.

front:
True or False?
Gamma decay usually occurs after alpha or beta decay when a nucleus has too much energy.
back:
True.
Gamma decay usually occurs after alpha or beta decay when a nucleus becomes excited and has too much energy.

front: What is the activity of a radioactive source?
back: Activity is the number of nuclei which decay in a given time. It is measured in becquerels.

front: What is 1 becquerel (Bq)?
back: One becquerel (Bq) is equivalent to a nucleus decaying every second.

front: What is the difference between activity and count rate?
back: Activity is the rate at which radiation is emitted, whereas count rate is the rate at which radiation is detected.

front: Define the term half-life.
back:
Half-life is the time taken for half the undecayed nuclei of a particular isotope in any sample to decay.
It is also the time taken for the activity of a source to fall to half its original value.

front:
True or False?
Different isotopes of the same element have the same half-life.
back:
False.
The half-life for a particular isotope is a constant value. Therefore, different isotopes have different half-lives.

front: What is the value of the activity of a radioactive sample after two half-lives?
back: The value of the activity of a radioactive sample after two half-lives is ¼ of its original value.

front: What proportion of original nuclei in a radioactive sample will remain after three half-lives?
back: After three half-lives, the proportion of original nuclei remaining in the sample will be ⅛.

front: How is the half-life of an isotope determined from a graph of activity against time?
back:
To determine the half-life of an isotope on a graph of activity over time:
• identify the point at which the activity has halved and draw a line to the curve
• track that point down to the time axis

front: What is the half-life of the following sample?
back:
The half-life of the sample is 5 hours:
• half-life is the time taken for the activity to fall to half its original value
• the time for the activity to fall from 800 to 400 counts per second is 5 hours

front: Name four uses of radioactivity.
back: Uses of radioactivity include: nuclear power; medicine e.g. radiotherapy, tracers and sterilising equipment; carbon dating; determining the age of rocks; detecting leaks in underground pipes; controlling the thickness of materials; smoke detectors

front: How can carbon dating be used to determine the age of once-living matter?
back: Carbon dating is a method used to determine the age of once-living matter by measuring the ratio of carbon-14 atoms to carbon-12 atoms that it contains; comparing this to the well-known ratio in living matter; using the half-life of carbon-14 to determine the time that has passed

front: How can uranium-lead dating be used to determine the age of the Earth?
back: Uranium-lead dating can be used to determine the age of the Earth by assuming the sample starts with 100% uranium and finishes with 100% lead; determining the percentage of these two elements in a rock; estimating the time since the decays started

front: What are the ideal properties of a radionuclide used for detecting leaks in underground pipes?
back:
The ideal properties of a radionuclide used for detecting leaks in underground pipes are:
• gamma emitter- this is the most penetrating type of radiation
• short half-life- activity needs to be at detectable levels but not for too long

front: Why is beta radiation used to monitor the thickness of materials?
back:
Beta radiation is used to monitor the thickness of materials because
• it can penetrate materials such as paper and aluminium foil
• the amount of beta radiation detected depends on the material thickness

front: Which type of radiation is used in smoke detectors?
back: Alpha radiation is used in smoke detectors.

front: Why is gamma radiation used in the treatment of cancer?
back:
Gamma radiation is used in radiotherapy (the treatment of cancer) because
• it can damage or kill cancerous cells
• it is penetrating enough to reach cancerous cells in the body

front: What is a radioactive tracer?
back: A radioactive tracer is a substance containing a radionuclide which is introduced into a system and tracked by detecting the radiation it emits.

front: What are the ideal properties of a radioactive tracer in medical imaging, such as technetium-99m?
back: The ideal properties of a radioactive tracer in medical imaging, such as technetium-99m are: gamma emitter- penetrating enough to be detected outside the body; short half-life- activity needs to be at detectable levels for the duration of the test, but not for long after

front: Why is gamma radiation used in the sterilisation of food and equipment?
back:
Gamma radiation is used in the sterilisation of food and equipment because
• it is highly penetrating, so it is able to irradiate entire surfaces
• it is ionising enough to kill bacteria and viruses

front: Define mass defect.
back: Mass defect is the difference between the mass of a nucleus and the total mass of all the constituent nucleons if they were separated.

front:
True or False?
Mass defect and binding energy are equivalent.
back:
True.
Mass defect and binding energy are equivalent.

front: Define nuclear binding energy.
back: Nuclear binding energy is the energy required to separate a nucleus into its constituent nucleons.

front: What causes a mass defect in the nucleus?
back: Mass defect is caused by the energy released when a nucleus forms, or the energy needed to separate all the nucleons in a nucleus.

front:
True or False?
A system of separate nucleons has a greater total mass than a system of nucleons bound in a nucleus.
back:
True.
A system of separated nucleons has a greater mass than a system of nucleons bound in a nucleus.

front:
True or False?
The term mass defect can be used to describe any change in mass that occurs in a nuclear reaction.
back:
False.
The term mass defect can only be used to describe the change in mass when all the nucleons are separated (equivalent to binding energy).
The decrease in mass which occurs during nuclear reactions (e.g. radioactive decay) should not be described as a mass defect.

front: What equation is used to convert mass to its equivalent energy?
back:
The equation used to convert mass to its equivalent energy is:              ΔE = Δm c²
Where:
• ΔE = change in energy, measured in joules (J)
• Δm = change in mass, or mass defect, measured in kilograms (kg)
• c = speed of light in a vacuum (3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)

front: Define atomic mass unit (u).
back: An atomic mass unit (u) is  the mass of a neutral atom of carbon-12.

front: Define binding energy per nucleon.
back: Binding energy per nucleon is the binding energy of a nucleus divided by the number of nucleons.

front:
True or False?
A low binding energy per nucleon means a nucleus is more stable.
back:
False.
A low binding energy per nucleon means a nucleus is less stable.
It means less energy would be required to separate the nucleons in the nucleus.

front: What does the steeper gradient at low values of A on the binding energy curve indicate?
back: The steeper gradient at low values of A indicates that fusion reactions release greater binding energy than fission reactions.

front: Why do heavy nuclei undergo fission?
back: Heavy nuclei undergo fission because they have high binding energies per nucleon, but this gradually decreases with A, making the heaviest elements the most unstable.

front:
True or False?
In both fusion and fission, the mass of the original nuclei is greater than the mass of the products.
back:
True.
In both fusion and fission, the mass of the original nuclei is greater than the mass of the products. This missing mass has been converted into energy.

front: What is the strong nuclear force?
back: The strong nuclear force is an attractive force which acts between nucleons and holds the nucleus together.

front: What is the range of the strong nuclear force?
back:
The range of the strong nuclear force is between 0.5 and 3.0 fm, where:
• it is repulsive below a separation of 0.5 fm
• it is attractive up to a separation of 3.0 fm

front: At what separation does the strong nuclear force have a maximum attractive value?
back: The strong nuclear force has its maximum attractive value at a separation of around 1.0 fm.

front: What is meant by the equilibrium position in terms of the strong nuclear force?
back: The equilibrium position is the point where the resultant force is zero and occurs at a separation of about 0.5 fm.

front:
True or False?
The composition of a nucleus changes following alpha, beta and gamma decay.
back:
False.
The composition of a nucleus changes following alpha and beta decay, but not following gamma decay.

front: What effect does alpha decay have on a nucleus?
back:
An alpha particle is a helium nucleus:
When a nucleus emits an alpha particle, the effect is:
• nucleon number decreases by 4
• proton number decreases by 2

front: What effect does beta-minus decay have on a nucleus?
back:
A beta-minus particle is an electron:
When a nucleus emits a beta-minus particle, the effect is:
• nucleon number stays the same
• proton number increases by 1

front: What effect does beta-plus decay have on a nucleus?
back:
A beta-plus particle is a positron:
When a nucleus emits a beta-plus particle, the effect is:
• nucleon number stays the same
• proton number decreases by 1

front: What effect does gamma decay have on a nucleus?
back:
Gamma radiation is electromagnetic radiation:
When a nucleus emits gamma radiation, the effect is:
• nucleon number stays the same
• proton number stays the same

front: List the three types of nuclear radiation in order of increasing ionising power.
back:
The types of nuclear radiation in order of increasing ionising power are:
• gamma (least ionising, creates fewest ion pairs per cm)
• beta (creates a moderate amount of ion pairs per cm)
• alpha (most ionising, creates most ion pairs per cm)

front: List the three types of nuclear radiation in order of increasing penetrating power.
back:
The types of nuclear radiation in order of increasing penetrating power are:
• alpha (least penetrating, can be stopped by paper)
• beta (can stopped by a few mm of aluminium)
• gamma (most penetrating, can be reduced by a few mm of lead)

front:
True or False?
Electron anti-neutrinos are emitted during beta-plus decay.
back:
False.
Electron anti-neutrinos are emitted during beta-minus decay.
Beta-minus decay is when a neutron turns into a proton and emits a beta-minus particle and an electron anti-neutrino.

front:
True or False?
An electron neutrino is emitted when a proton turns into a neutron.
back:
True.
An electron neutrino is emitted along with a beta-plus particle when a proton turns into a neutron.

front:
True or False?
Nuclei with too many neutrons decay by either beta-minus decay or beta-plus decay.
back:
False.
Nuclei with too many neutrons decay by beta-minus decay only.

front:
True or False?
Nuclei with too many protons decay by either beta-plus decay or electron capture.
back:
True.
Nuclei with too many protons decay by either beta-plus decay or electron capture.

front:
True or False?
Alpha decay usually occurs in small unstable nuclei.
back:
False.
Nuclei with too many nucleons (protons and neutrons) decay by alpha decay.
Therefore, alpha decay usually occurs in very large unstable nuclei.

front:
True or False?
Gamma decay usually occurs after alpha or beta decay when a nucleus has too much energy.
back:
True.
Gamma decay usually occurs after alpha or beta decay when a nucleus becomes excited and has too much energy.

front: What is the activity of a radioactive source?
back: Activity is the number of nuclei which decay in a given time. It is measured in becquerels.

front: What is 1 becquerel (Bq)?
back: One becquerel (Bq) is equivalent to a nucleus decaying every second.

front: What is the difference between activity and count rate?
back: Activity is the rate at which radiation is emitted, whereas count rate is the rate at which radiation is detected.

front: Define the term half-life.
back:
Half-life is the time taken for half the undecayed nuclei of a particular isotope in any sample to decay.
It is also the time taken for the activity of a source to fall to half its original value.

front:
True or False?
Different isotopes of the same element have the same half-life.
back:
False.
The half-life for a particular isotope is a constant value. Therefore, different isotopes have different half-lives.

front: What is the value of the activity of a radioactive sample after two half-lives?

back:

• identify the point at which the activity has halved and draw a line to the curve
• track that point down to the time axis

• the time for the activity to fall from 800 to 400 counts per second is 5 hours

back: The decay constant is the probability that an individual nucleus will decay per unit of time.

front:
True or False?
A radionuclide with a short half-life will decay at a slower rate.
back:
False.
A radionuclide with a short half-life will decay at a faster rate.
The shorter the half-life of a radionuclide, the greater the decay constant and activity.

front: Why does the activity of a sample decrease over time?
back:
The activity of a sample decreases over time because:
• unstable nuclei emit radiation to become more stable
• after each decay, the number of unstable nuclei remaining decreases
• activity is directly proportional to the number of nuclei, so activity decreases

front: What is exponential decay?
back: Exponential decay is when the rate of change of a quantity decreases at a constant rate.

front:
True or False?
In radioactive decay, the number of undecayed nuclei never reaches zero.
back:
True.
The number of undecayed nuclei never reaches zero in radioactive decay.

front: How does the number of undecayed nuclei in a radioactive sample vary with time?
back: The number of undecayed nuclei in a radioactive sample decreases exponentially with time.

front:
True or False?
The steeper the slope of a decay curve, the smaller the decay constant.
back:
False.
The steeper the slope of a decay curve, the greater the decay constant.

front: What does the y-intercept of a decay curve represent?
back:
The y-intercept of a decay curve represents the initial value of the measured quantity, such as
•  N0  = initial number of undecayed nuclei
•  A0  = initial activity of the sample (Bq)
•  C0 = initial count rate (cpm)

front: Name four uses of radioactivity.
back:
Uses of radioactivity include:
• nuclear power
• medicine e.g. radiotherapy, tracers and sterilising equipment
• carbon dating
• determining the age of rocks
• detecting leaks in underground pipes
• controlling the thickness of materials
• smoke detectors

front: How can carbon dating be used to determine the age of once-living matter?
back:
Carbon dating is a method used to determine the age of once-living matter by
• measuring the ratio of carbon-14 atoms to carbon-12 atoms that it contains
• comparing this to the well-known ratio in living matter
• using the half-life of carbon-14 to determine the time that has passed

front: How can uranium-lead dating be used to determine the age of the Earth?
back:
Uranium-lead dating can be used to determine the age of the Earth by
• assuming the sample starts with 100% uranium and finishes with 100% lead
• determining the percentage of these two elements in a rock
• estimating the time since the decays started

front: What are the ideal properties of a radionuclide used for detecting leaks in underground pipes?
back:
The ideal properties of a radionuclide used for detecting leaks in underground pipes are:
• gamma emitter - this is the most penetrating type of radiation
• short half-life - activity needs to be at detectable levels but not for too long

front: Why is beta radiation used to monitor the thickness of materials?
back:
Beta radiation is used to monitor the thickness of materials because
• it can penetrate materials such as paper and aluminium foil
• the amount of beta radiation detected depends on the material thickness

front: Which type of radiation is used in smoke detectors?
back: Alpha radiation is used in smoke detectors.

front: Why is gamma radiation used in the treatment of cancer?
back:
Gamma radiation is used in radiotherapy (the treatment of cancer) because
• it can damage or kill cancerous cells
• it is penetrating enough to reach cancerous cells in the body

front: What is a radioactive tracer?
back: A radioactive tracer is a substance containing a radionuclide which is introduced into a system and tracked by detecting the radiation it emits.

front: What are the ideal properties of a radioactive tracer in medical imaging, such as technetium-99m?
back:
The ideal properties of a radioactive tracer in medical imaging, such as technetium-99m are:
• gamma emitter - penetrating enough to be detected outside the body
• short half-life - activity needs to be at detectable levels for the duration of the test, but not for long after

front: Why is gamma radiation used in the sterilisation of food and equipment?
back:
Gamma radiation is used in the sterilisation of food and equipment because
• it is highly penetrating, so it is able to irradiate entire surfaces
• it is ionising enough to kill bacteria and viruses

front: Define mass defect.
back: Mass defect is the difference between the mass of a nucleus and the total mass of all the constituent nucleons if they were separated.

front:
True or False?
Mass defect and binding energy are equivalent.
back:
True.
Mass defect and binding energy are equivalent.

front: Define nuclear binding energy.
back: Nuclear binding energy is the energy required to separate a nucleus into its constituent nucleons.

front: What causes a mass defect in the nucleus?
back: Mass defect is caused by the energy released when a nucleus forms, or the energy needed to separate all the nucleons in a nucleus.

front:
True or False?
A system of separate nucleons has a greater total mass than a system of nucleons bound in a nucleus.
back:
True.
A system of separated nucleons has a greater mass than a system of nucleons bound in a nucleus.

front:
True or False?
The term mass defect can be used to describe any change in mass that occurs in a nuclear reaction.
back:
False.
The term mass defect can only be used to describe the change in mass when all the nucleons are separated (equivalent to binding energy).
The decrease in mass which occurs during nuclear reactions (e.g. radioactive decay) should not be described as a mass defect.

front: Define atomic mass unit (u).
back: An atomic mass unit (u) is    the mass of a neutral atom of carbon-12.

front: Define binding energy per nucleon.
back: Binding energy per nucleon is the binding energy of a nucleus divided by the number of nucleons.

front:
True or False?
A low binding energy per nucleon means a nucleus is more stable.
back:
False.
A low binding energy per nucleon means a nucleus is less stable.
It means less energy would be required to separate the nucleons in the nucleus.

front: What does the steeper gradient at low values of A on the binding energy curve indicate?
back: The steeper gradient at low values of A indicates that fusion reactions release greater binding energy than fission reactions.

front: Why do heavy nuclei undergo fission?
back: Heavy nuclei undergo fission because they have high binding energies per nucleon, but this gradually decreases with A, making the heaviest elements the most unstable.

front:
True or False?
In both fusion and fission, the mass of the original nuclei is greater than the mass of the products.
back:
True.
In both fusion and fission, the mass of the original nuclei is greater than the mass of the products. This missing mass has been converted into energy.

front: What is the strong nuclear force?
back: The strong nuclear force is an attractive force which acts between nucleons and holds the nucleus together.

front: What is the range of the strong nuclear force?
back:
The range of the strong nuclear force is between 0.5 and 3.0 fm, where:
• it is repulsive below a separation of 0.5 fm
• it is attractive up to a separation of 3.0 fm

front: At what separation does the strong nuclear force have a maximum attractive value?
back: The strong nuclear force has its maximum attractive value at a separation of around 1.0 fm.

front: What is meant by the equilibrium position in terms of the strong nuclear force?
back: The equilibrium position is the point where the resultant force is zero and occurs at a separation of about 0.5 fm.

front: What does the line of stability show on a nuclear stability curve?
back: The line of stability shows N and Z values that produce stable nuclei.

front: What makes a nucleus unstable?
back:
A nucleus will be unstable if it has:
• too many neutrons
• too many protons
• too many nucleons (protons and neutrons)
• too much energy

front:
True or False?
The neutron-to-proton ratio for stable light isotopes (Z < 20) is about 1.
back:
True.
The neutron-to-proton ratio for stable light isotopes (Z < 20) is about 1.
This means these nuclei usually contain equal numbers of protons and neutrons.

front: How does the neutron-proton ratio change for heavy isotopes (Z > 20)?
back:
For heavy isotopes (Z > 20), the neutron-proton ratio increases up to a maximum of around 1.5.
This means these nuclei can contain up to 50% more neutrons than protons.

front: Why do heavy isotopes need more neutrons than protons to be stable?
back: Heavy isotopes need more neutrons than protons to be stable to add distance between protons to reduce the effects of electrostatic repulsion.

front: How are nuclear energy levels similar to electron energy levels?
back: Nuclear energy levels are similar to electron energy levels in that nuclei can exist in excited states and emit energy as photons when transitioning to lower states.

front:
True or False?
The nucleus emits gamma rays with a continuous range of energies.
back:
False.
The nucleus emits gamma rays with a range of discrete energies.

front: What happens when a nucleus changes from an excited state to a lower energy level?
back: When a nucleus changes from an excited state to a lower energy level, a gamma-ray photon will be emitted.

front:
True or False?
Alpha particles emitted from the same radionuclide possess a range of discrete energies.
back:
True.
Alpha particles emitted from the same radionuclide possess a range of discrete energies.

front: What do the spectra of alpha and gamma radiation provide evidence for?
back: The spectra of alpha and gamma radiation provide evidence for discrete nuclear energy levels.

front:
True or False?
Beta particles emitted from the same radionuclide possess a range of discrete energies.
back:
False.
Beta particles emitted from the same radionuclide possess a continuous range of energies.

front: What does the curve in the beta particle energy distribution graph indicate?
back: The curve in the beta particle energy distribution graph indicates that the energy released in beta decay is shared between the beta particle and neutrino (or anti-neutrino).

front: How do alpha and beta emissions differ in terms of energy distribution?
back: Alpha particles are emitted with discrete energies, while beta particles have a continuous range of energies.

front: What does the continuous spectrum of beta decay provide evidence for?
back: The continuous spectrum of beta decay provides evidence for the neutrino.

front: Define nuclear fission.
back: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large nucleus into two smaller nuclei.

front: What is spontaneous fission?
back: Spontaneous fission occurs randomly and without additional energy being put into the nucleus.

front: What is induced fission?
back: Induced fission occurs when a stable nucleus splits into small nuclei due to the absorption of a thermal (slow-moving) neutron.

front:
True or False?
Uranium-235 is an example of a fissile material.
back:
True.
Uranium-235 is an example of a fissile material, this means it can undergo fission reactions - its nuclei can be split apart into smaller nuclei.

front:
True or False?
More than one neutron is required to induce fission in a uranium-235 nucleus.
back:
False.
Only one neutron is required to induce fission in a uranium-235 nucleus.

front: What happens when a uranium-235 nucleus is bombarded with fast-moving neutrons?
back: When a uranium-235 nucleus is bombarded with fast-moving neutrons, they will rebound and fission will not be induced

front: In what form is energy released from nuclear fission reactions?
back: In fission reactions, energy is released in the form of kinetic energy of the fragments as well as neutrons and gamma rays.

front:
True or False?
In a nuclear fission reaction, the mass of the daughter nuclei is the same as the mass of the parent nucleus
back:
False.
In a nuclear fission reaction, the mass of the daughter nuclei is less than the mass of the parent nucleus.

front:
True or False?
For nuclear fission to occur, the fission fragments must be more stable than the original nucleus.
back:
True.
For nuclear fission to occur, the fission fragments must be more stable than the original nucleus.
In other words, the fission fragments must have higher values of binding energy per nucleon than the original nucleus undergoing fission.

front:
True or False?
Nuclear fission has a similar energy density to other sources of fuel.
back:
False.
Nuclear fission has the highest energy density of any currently used fuel source.

front: What is a nuclear chain reaction?
back: A nuclear chain reaction occurs when: 2 or 3 neutrons are emitted from a fission reaction; these neutrons cause further fission reactions; more neutrons are emitted; the rate of fission reactions increases

front: What is a thermal neutron?
back: A thermal neutron is a neutron which is in thermal equilibrium with the moderator.

front:
True or False?
For every fission reaction, there is, on average, one further fission reaction.
back:
True.
When the rate of fission is constant, each fission reaction goes on to initiate, on average, one further fission reaction.

front: What happens if the amount of nuclear fuel in a fission reactor is too low?
back:
If the amount of nuclear fuel in a fission reactor is below the critical mass, chain reactions will stop or slow down.
This is because neutrons can escape the material without hitting any more nuclei.

front: What happens if the amount of nuclear fuel in a fission reactor is too high?
back:
If the amount of nuclear fuel in a fission reactor is above the critical mass, chain reactions increase rapidly.
If uncontrolled, this can lead to a huge release of energy and even a nuclear explosion.

front: What is the purpose of control rods in a nuclear reactor?
back: The purpose of control rods is to absorb neutrons.

front: What is the purpose of the moderator in a nuclear reactor?
back: The purpose of a moderator is to slow down neutrons.

front: Why must neutrons be slowed down in a nuclear reactor?
back:
In a nuclear reactor, neutrons must be slowed down so they can react with the uranium fuel efficiently.
This is because slow neutrons are more likely to be absorbed by a uranium nucleus than fast neutrons.

front:
True or False?
Lowering the control rods in a nuclear reactor increases the rate of fission.
back:
False.
Lowering the control rods decreases the rate of fission as more neutrons are absorbed.

front: What is the purpose of shielding in a nuclear reactor?
back: The purpose of shielding is to absorb hazardous radiation.

front: What is nuclear waste?
back:
Nuclear waste refers to the leftover radioactive materials associated with the production of nuclear power. Different waste materials can be classed as
• low-level waste
• intermediate-level waste
• high-level waste

front: How is low-level nuclear waste treated?
back:
Low-level nuclear waste is treated by:
• encasing it in drums filled with concrete
• storing it underground for a few years
• eventually disposing of it in landfill sites

front: How is intermediate-level nuclear waste treated?
back:
Intermediate-level nuclear waste is treated by:
• encasing it in steel drums filled with concrete
• storing it underground in a secured facility

front: How is high-level nuclear waste treated?
back: High-level nuclear waste is treated by: recovering useable isotopes of uranium and plutonium; encasing it in reinforced steel containers filled with concrete or vitrified with molten glass; storing in underwater cooling tanks initially; storing it deep underground in a secured facility

front: Is contaminated clothing classified as low, intermediate, or high-level waste?
back: Contaminated clothing is classified as low-level waste.

front: Are spent fuel rods classified as low, intermediate, or high-level waste?
back: Spent fuel rods are classified as high-level waste.

front: What are the advantages of nuclear power?
back:
Some of the advantages of nuclear power are:
• it produces no greenhouse gases or chemical pollution
• it is a highly reliable method of electricity generation
• nuclear fuel is widely available and has an extremely high energy density

front: What are the disadvantages of nuclear power?
back: Some of the disadvantages of nuclear power are: it produces hazardous radioactive waste with a long half-life (or high activity); the cost of building, operating and de-commissioning reactors is very high; there is a (low) threat of serious accidents

front: What is nuclear fusion?
back: Nuclear fusion is the joining of two smaller nuclei to form one larger nucleus, releasing a large amount of energy in the process.

front: Where does nuclear fusion take place in stars?
back: Nuclear fusion takes place in the centres (cores) of stars.

front: Why do nuclei require very high kinetic energies in order to fuse?
back:
Nuclei require very high kinetic energies to fuse to
• overcome the repulsive coulomb forces between protons
• get close enough for the strong nuclear force to act

front: In what form is energy released from nuclear fusion reactions?
back: In fusion reactions, energy is released in the form of kinetic energy of the nuclei produced as well as gamma rays and neutrinos.

front:
True or False?
In a nuclear fusion reaction, the mass of the fused nucleus is the same as the mass of the two nuclei that fused together.
back:
False.
In a nuclear fusion reaction, the mass of the fused nucleus is less than the mass of the two nuclei that fused together. The remaining mass has been converted to energy.

front:
True or False?
Fission reactions release more energy per kg than fusion reactions.
back:
False.
Fusion reactions release much more energy per kg than fission.

front: What two conditions are required for nuclear fusion to occur?
back:
The two conditions required for nuclear fusion to occur are:
• High temperature
• High pressure or density

front: What is radiation pressure?
back: Radiation pressure is a pressure that arises due to the transfer of momentum from photons to the surrounding matter.

front: How do main sequence stars remain in equilibrium?
back: Main sequence stars remain in equilibrium because fusion reactions generate radiation pressure which acts outwards and balances the inwards-acting gravitational force.

front: When does a protostar become a main sequence star?
back: A protostar becomes a main sequence star when nuclear fusion reactions are initiated in its core and the inward force of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure from the fusion reactions.

front:
True or False?
All stars form from a cloud of dust and gas which becomes a protostar and then a main sequence star.
back:
True.
All stars follow the same initial stages in their life cycle:
• Nebula (cloud of dust and gas)
• Protostar
• Main sequence star
The stages that follow depend on the mass of the main sequence star that forms.

front: Name the stages, in the correct order, in the life cycle of a star similar to the Sun.
back: The stages, in the correct order, in the life cycle of a star similar to the Sun are: Nebula (cloud of dust and gas); Protostar; Main sequence star; Red giant; Planetary nebula; White dwarf

front: When does a main sequence star turn into a red giant?
back: A main sequence star turns into a red giant when hydrogen in the star's core begins to run out and the star begins to fuse helium into heavier elements.

front:
True or False?
A high-mass star will eventually explode as a supernova and become a white dwarf.
back:
False.
A high mass star will eventually explode as a supernova and become a neutron star or a black hole.

front: Name the stages, in the correct order, in the life cycle of a star with a mass larger than the Sun.
back: The stages, in the correct order, in the life cycle of a star with a mass larger than the Sun are: Nebula (cloud of dust and gas); Protostar; Main sequence; Red supergiant; Supernova; Black hole, or neutron star

front: What is a supernova?
back: A supernova is a large exploding star.

front: Under what conditions does a supernova occur?
back: A supernova occurs when a star much more massive than the Sun reaches the end of its red supergiant stage. It collapses, becomes very unstable and explodes.

front: What determines whether the remnant core of a massive star becomes a neutron star or a black hole?
back: The mass of the remnant core determines whether a massive star becomes a neutron star or a black hole.

front:
True or False?
High-mass stars have significantly longer lifetimes than low-mass stars.
back:
False.
High-mass stars have significantly shorter lifetimes than low-mass stars.
The greater the mass of a star, the higher its temperature, therefore, the greater the rate of fusion and the quicker the fuel is depleted in its core.

front: What is a Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram?
back: The Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram is a plot of a star's luminosity on the y-axis and its surface temperature on the x-axis.

front: Which star on the H-R diagram has the highest surface temperature, A, B, C or D?
back:
The star with the highest surface temperature is star B.
The hottest stars are located towards the left side of the H-R diagram.

front: Which star on the H-R diagram has the lowest surface temperature, A, B, C or D?
back:
The star with the coolest surface temperature is star D.
The coolest stars are located towards the right side of the H-R diagram.

front: Which star on the H-R diagram is the brightest, A, B, C or D?
back:
The brightest star is star A.
The brightest stars are found near the top of the H-R diagram.

front: Which star on the H-R diagram is most similar to the Sun, A, B, C or D?
back:
The most similar star to the Sun is star C.
The luminosity scale is given in solar units, where the luminosity of the Sun = 1

front: Where is the main sequence located on the H-R diagram?
back: On the H-R diagram, main sequence stars are stars found in a band from the top left to the bottom right.

front: Where are white dwarfs located on the H-R diagram?
back: On the H-R diagram, white dwarfs are located below the main sequence and slightly to the left.

front: Where are red giants located on the H-R diagram?
back: On the H-R diagram, red giants are located above the main sequence and slightly to the right.

front: What type of stars are the hottest and dimmest on the H-R diagram?
back: The hottest and dimmest stars on the H-R diagram are white dwarfs.

front: What type of stars are the coolest and brightest on the H-R diagram?
back: The coolest and brightest stars on the H-R diagram are red supergiants.

front: What are the three types of light spectra?
back:
The three types of light spectra are:
• continuous spectra
• emission spectra
• absorption spectra

front:
True or False?
Absorption spectra are observed when white light passes through a hot, low-pressure gas.
back:
False.
Absorption spectra are observed when white light passes through a cool, low-pressure gas.

front:
True or False?
Continuous spectra are produced by hot, dense sources.
back:
True.
Continuous spectra are produced from hot, dense sources, such as the cores of stars.

front: Why do stars emit absorption spectra?
back:
Stars emit absorption spectra because:
• the hot, dense core produces a continuous spectrum
• the cool, low-density gas in the outer layers absorbs photons
• the resulting spectrum is a set of dark lines on a coloured background

front: How can the chemical composition of a star be determined?
back: The chemical composition of a star can be determined by analyzing its absorption spectrum and identifying elements by their unique pattern of spectral lines.

front: Define 1 astronomical unit (AU).
back:
One astronomical unit (AU) is the mean distance between the centre of the Earth and the centre of the Sun.
1 AU is equal to approximately 1.5 × 10¹¹ m.

front: Define 1 light-year (ly).
back:
One light-year is the distance travelled by light in one year.
1 ly is equal to approximately 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m.

front: Define 1 parsec (pc).
back:
One parsec is a unit of distance that gives a parallax angle of 1 second of an arc.
1 pc is equal to approximately 3.1 × 10¹⁶ m.

front: What is stellar parallax?
back: Stellar parallax is the displacement in the apparent position of a nearby star against a background of distant stars when viewed from different positions of the Earth during its orbit around the Sun.

front:
True or False?
Stellar parallax is accurate for measuring distances up to about 100 light-years.
back:
False.
Stellar parallax is accurate for measuring distances up to about 100 parsecs.

The parallax angle increases as the distance to a star increases.
